Autumn
2026
Ramsey Town Council
Residents Communication
RAMSEY COMMUNITIES NEIGHBOURHOOD PLAN
A further step forward
The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan has been prepared with local voices at the heart. People
gave their opinions via consultation over the summer of 2025 and the plan was then put together by a
steering group of residents before going back out as a draft for further consultation. We’re pleased to say
that it has also passed another significant step - Independent Assessment.
Further details can be found on the Ramsey Town Council website.
What happens next?
The next major step will be a community vote
through a referendum organised by
Huntingdonshire District Council, likely to be in
December 2026. It will be organised in the same
way as an election and everyone on the electoral
register will be notified. You will be asked whether
you accept the Neighbourhood Plan - yes or no.
We will produce a quick reference guide for anyone
who may not have time to read the full document.
Key points include:
Providing new infrastructure, facilities and
services so new development benefits existing,
new and future residents.
Supporting a vibrant community with places to
live, work, stay and play, including affordable
housing and housing with a local connection.
Protecting the historic environment, heritage
assets and green spaces that matter to the
community.
Having our Neighbourhood Plan in place will mean Ramsey
receives 25% of developer contributions rather than the
current 15%.
That means more money can be spent directly in our
community.
neighbourhood.plan@ramseytowncouncil.gov.uk

CIL - Community Infrastructure Levy
What is CIL? Community Infrastructure Levy, commonly referred to as CIL, is money collected by
Huntingdonshire District Council from certain new developments. The funding is then used to help
provide or improve infrastructure needed as communities grow.
The money collected is broadly divided into three areas:
Up to 5% can be retained by Huntingdonshire District Council towards the administration and
collection of CIL.
15% is normally allocated to the Town or Parish Council for the area where the development takes
place. Once an adopted Neighbourhood Plan is in place, this increases to 25%.
Most of the remaining funding is retained by Huntingdonshire District Council for larger strategic
infrastructure projects across the district.
Ramsey Town Council currently receives the 15% neighbourhood portion. Once the Ramsey
Communities Neighbourhood Plan is adopted, this will increase to 25%, giving the Council a greater
share of money from qualifying development to invest back into our communities.
Current projects supported or earmarked through Ramsey Town Council’s CIL funding include:
Improvements at The Moorings.
Contributions towards Local Highways Improvement projects.
Improvements to Newtown Road Play Park.
Improvements to the public toilets.
New benches at the skate park.
CCTV at The Moorings and New Road.
The Double Yellow Lines project.
The Town Council is also considering future projects, including additional parking behind the doctor’s
surgery at Mews Close.
Local Highways Initiative Bid (LHI): what is an LHI?
The Local Highway Improvement programme allows local councils and community organisations to
apply to Cambridgeshire County Council for funding towards highway improvements. Projects can
include new or extended footpaths, traffic-calming measures, speed-reduction schemes, and other
changes designed to improve road and pedestrian safety.
Ramsey Town Council identifies potential projects and submits applications to Cambridgeshire County
Council. Applications are assessed by the County Council and, if successful, funding is awarded
towards the cost of the scheme. Under the current scheme, up to £25,000 can be awarded towards
more complex projects, with applicants expected to contribute at least 10% of the overall cost.
One recent LHI project was the extension of the footpath along Stocking Fen Road towards the
industrial estate, improving pedestrian access for people travelling to and from work. The Council has
also submitted an application for speed-reduction measures on the approach to Ramsey St Mary’s and
is awaiting the outcome.
Abbey College Road Safety Campaign
Abbey College students are raising funds towards the £10,000 needed to help
pay for speed reduction measures on Hollow Lane. Students have been
campaigning, the school submitted an LHI bid, and speed cushions are
planned. They would be grateful if you could spare the price of a coffee and
scan the QR code.

Message from the Mayor of Ramsey
Hello everyone, I hope you’ve all had a wonderful summer. Personally, I can’t
believe how quickly this year has flown by and that, as I write this, we’re already
going into autumn. 
I want to use this column to recognise some amazing people - the Ramsey
Town Council staff team, led by our Clerk, Lisa Renfree. They have had an
incredibly busy summer, with lots of change and new initiatives to contend with
as our Council grows and new Councillors come on board with the ambition to
achieve and deliver more for our residents.
They organised the Bands on the Green programme, delivered a family fun day at QEII Park with
entertainment from the Blues Brothers and Queen tribute acts, produced and managed delivery of our
newsletters to 5,000 homes, and got to grips with a new finance system. This was all on top of day-to-
day customer service and administration, room bookings, council meetings and communications. They
also stepped up to help coordinate meals and drinks for firefighters at Holme Fen during the recent
wildfire, when the RRT Charity had to leave after a week.
They do all of this professionally and with a smile. More often, however, they are facing abusive
behaviour and, as a Council, this is something we will not tolerate. We have had to notify the police
and use CCTV as evidence. Thankfully, this behaviour comes from a minority, and I know many of you
appreciate the time our staff takes to assist you. So, from me and all fellow Councillors: thank you Lisa,
Amanda, Kay, Alison, Quincy, Morgan and Paul - you are appreciated. Keep up the great work for our
community.
Thank you, Ramsey Parish community and beyond
On behalf of Ramsey Town Council, we would like to thank
everyone who supported the firefighters responding to the fire at
Holme Fen. The response from local businesses, organisations
and volunteers was incredible. Our thanks go to The Farmers
Coffee Shop, Gorilla Pizza and Friar Tuck Fish & Chips for
providing food and support; Ramsey Community Centre for
opening its kitchen to prepare the large quantity of meals needed;
The Admiral Wells for becoming a hub of activity, preparing meals
and acting as a donation drop-off point; and Stevelyn & Creative
Crafters for also providing a collection point, to name just a few.
We would also like to thank the many volunteers who gave their time to prepare food and help
wherever needed, as well as everyone who made donations. The JustGiving appeal raised an amazing
£4,546.56. The Mayor also had the privilege of meeting The Duke of Gloucester during his visit to
Holme Fen, where he saw the devastation caused by the fire and personally thanked firefighters, the
owners of The Admiral Wells and local volunteers for their incredible efforts.
The Lord-Lieutenant, Julie Spence, who accompanied him, spoke of how proud
she was to see the community come together so quickly and effectively.
Firefighters expressed their appreciation for every meal, drink and homemade
cake provided during the response.
Following the fire, a meeting of local community groups has been arranged for 1
October to discuss emergency planning and how the community can work
together in response to future major incidents.

Meet the new Town Council members
My husband and I chose Ramsey 26 years ago based on what we felt it had to
offer us as a family and our growing children: the wonderful people, the community,
the facilities, the coffee shops, the leisure centre and the parks. There have been
many changes since then, and I want to make sure Ramsey remains that
wonderful place. Hopefully, my role as a magistrate, my previous experience with
numerous community groups and the experience of raising my children in this
community will stand me in good stead to help the people of Ramsey further.
If you have opinions about the community in which you live, then for me, it is
important to express them in a positive way by becoming involved in the decision-
making forums and involving yourself actively and practically in the implementation
of ideas. In addition, having benefited from living in Ramsey for many years, I also
felt that it was time to repay some of those benefits by contributing, in some small
part, to the development of our community. I therefore took a leap of faith earlier
this year and put my name forward for election to the town council.
 
My family and I moved to Ramsey two years ago, and what began as a new
chapter has become home. With my daughter attending school locally, I have seen
how important a connected, inclusive community is. I want her to grow up
somewhere people feel proud to call home. Throughout my career, including my
recent role in strategic transformation and programme management at M&S, I have
developed strong skills in collaboration, listening and turning ideas into action. I
want to bring these values to Ramsey, listening to residents and supporting our
town’s continued growth. Please say hello and share your thoughts when you see
me around town. 
Freedom of the Town – Pat Taylor
Freedom of the Town is the highest honour a Town Council can
award. On Sunday 20th September 2026, it was awarded to Pat
Taylor for her commitment to Ramsey.
Pat was an English teacher for many years and has taught lots of
residents; however, her volunteering means that she is also
known in many other capacities, spread across the years.
She was a Trustee of Ramsey Welfare Charities and Jones
Court, supporting our older residents; she volunteered at the
foodbank, where Reverend Richard Darmody said her help and
support were invaluable.
Council meeting dates - All residents are welcome
Ramsey Town Council meets on the second Thursday of every month at 7 pm in the Council Building
on Great Whyte. Residents are welcome to listen and have an opportunity at the start of the meeting to
address Council members.
8 October · 12 November · 10 December · 14 January · 11 February · 11 March
8 April · 13 May (AGM) · 10 June · 8 July · 12 August · 9 September
Pat was part of the steering committee that helped to form Ramsey U3A, and she was the first Chair
from 2011 to 2012, remaining a member to the present day.
She has also been a Town Councillor, serving for 26 years until her recent retirement, and has been
Mayor of Ramsey twice.
Her nomination for the Freedom of Ramsey was put forward by Cllr Adela Costello and was
wholeheartedly approved by fellow Councillors. Our congratulations to Pat; thank you for all you have
done to support our community.
Cllr Webster
Cllr Axelsen
Cllr Thompson

Public Toilets - New Road
The Moorings
It has been lovely to see residents and young people making use of
the improvements at The Moorings, including young people fishing
and spending time with friends.
Ramsey Town Council is also working with Ramsey Rotary to
introduce crocuses and other planting to bring more colour to the
area. The improvements at The Moorings have been funded through
the Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL). 
Ramsey Town Council is currently replacing the doors at the public toilets and has installed a payment
facility, which will come into operation once the refurbishment works are complete. The Council has
decided to introduce a small charge for use of the facilities to reduce anti-social behaviour and help
ensure the toilets remain clean and in good condition. CCTV will also be installed on New Road to help
identify those responsible for anti-social behaviour and to support Huntingdonshire District Council and
the police in dealing with incidents.
Skate Park Benches and No to Floodlights
As we go to print, the Council is selecting and arranging new picnic benches to be installed near the
skate park, ready for spring 2027. These, together with the new concrete rumble-strip area, are
expected to be in place in October and some grass seeding will continue to improve the area for young
people and residents.
There has recently been incorrect information circulating on social media suggesting that the Council is
considering floodlighting at the skate park. This is not the case. When the Council agreed to the skate
park, it was clear that the facility should not be encouraged for use after dark. This also reflects
feedback from nearby residents who have contacted the Clerk and Councillors with concerns about the
potential for increased anti-social behaviour during the evening.
Newtown Road Under-5s Play Park Improvement
Residents will have seen that the new fencing to extend the under-5s play area has now been
completed. The public consultation has also been launched and shared with residents and nurseries
across the Ramsey area. Ramsey Town Council has listened to feedback from families with young
children about the limited amount of play equipment currently available and the need to update the
existing facilities.
With a growing number of young families in the area, the Council felt it was important to make
Newtown Road Play Park a priority, particularly as other play parks across the town have benefited
from new equipment over the last three years.

Bands on the Green 2026
Bands on the Green has been really successful. The
weather was very kind to us - sometimes almost too hot!
It was good to have some new bands join us this year,
including the Abbey College Band and Janine Mitchell
singing. Ramsey Town Council would like to thank the
team of volunteers at St Thomas a Becket Church for
supplying teas, coffee and scrumptious cake.
Heritage Day - Sunday 13 September
Heritage Day was very popular this year, and it
was wonderful to meet people from as far away as
Berkshire and Essex. The Heritage Partnership
funded reenactments of the Vikings, the Sealed
Knot, and the Romans. Luckily, the Mayor
survived the stocks!
Heritage Day showcases our history: Ramsey Rural Museum, Victorian Walled Garden, Abbey
Gatehouse, St Thomas a Becket Church and the Mortuary Chapels.
The Hangout - Youth Club every Thursday
Ramsey Neighbourhoods Trust has launched its youth club, The
Hangout. It is open to all young people aged 11+ and is held at
the Pavilion on Cricketfield Lane. The youth club is open from
6.15pm to 7.45pm every Thursday during term time. Ramsey
Town Council is pleased to fund the youth club.
Youth Café has opened again and runs every Monday from
3.30pm to 6pm at The Farmers Café. It is free to attend, tuck is
available, and it provides a safe place to hang out with friends.
BOSH is the club for younger people. It is held every Thursday during term time from 4.30pm to 6pm,
offering children fun and games.

Rotary in Ramsey
Anti-Social Behaviour - How to Report
Ramsey Town Council has recently received several requests for CCTV cameras in different areas of
the community following concerns about anti-social behaviour.
Reports of anti-social behaviour should be made to Huntingdonshire District Council. Reporting
incidents is important because it helps build an accurate picture of where problems are occurring and
provides the evidence needed for the relevant authorities to take action.
Anti-social behaviour can be reported online at:
forms.huntingdonshire.gov.uk/REPORTANTISOCIALBEHAVIOUR/launch
Alternatively, email communityaction@huntingdonshire.gov.uk or call 01480 388388.
One-to-one meeting with a Councillor
If you would like to speak to a Councillor on a one-to-one basis about a local
issue, concern, or idea, appointments can be arranged throughout the week,
including evenings and weekends.
This allows residents to discuss matters directly with a Councillor at a time
that is convenient for them.
Simply scan the QR code, complete the short form and request an
appointment. A suitable time can then be arranged with you.
Ramsey Business Forum
Ramsey Town Council is launching its first Business Forum on Tuesday 13 October at 6pm at The
George, Ramsey. 
The forum will give local businesses a direct opportunity to raise concerns, share ideas, and help
shape the Council’s new Economic Development work, focused on increasing footfall and supporting
local businesses.
All Businesses are welcome.
Ramsey Town Council is pleased to continue its close
relationship with Rotary in Ramsey. The Clerk and Rotary’s
Secretary regularly meet to share information and work
together on events.
The Council looks forward to hosting one of the Santa Float evenings
for the volunteers after they have been out raising funds.
To get involved, contact
secretary@ramseyrotary.co.uk and book to
attend the planning evening on Wednesday 11
November.
Look out for the Santa Tracker to find
out when he will visit your street.

Raising funds for the Mayor’s
charities: Ramsey Rural Museum and
the Armed Services Veterans
Breakfast Club.
No experience is needed - trust the
process and you will have loads of fun
and create a wonderful item.
Click the QR code to book or email
events@ramseytowncouncil.gov.uk
.
Events for you to come along and enjoy
Scan the QR code
to donate. Every
pound is very much
appreciated.
Ramsey Christmas Lights is putting the
tree up on Saturday 14 November.
Complete the festive trail to collect your
bauble, decorate it and have it hung on the
tree. That afternoon there will be a children’s
Christmas Party, a chance to have a family
photograph taken by a professional
photographer, Santa in his grotto for a selfie
and a Snow Globe. The party is free and will
be held at Ramsey Community Centre, with
refreshments on sale.
Switch-On Day - Saturday 28 November. The morning
starts at 10am at Abbey College with the Christmas
Bazaar. The town-centre switch-on starts at 3pm with a
Taylor Swift tribute, and the lights go on at 5.15pm. The
fairground will be in town until 8pm. There is an envelope
with this newsletter, or you can scan the QR code above.
Festive Markets
Saturday 5 December
Saturday 12 December
Saturday 19 December
To book a stall, contact:
events@ramseytowncouncil.gov.uk
Festive Extravaganza
Saturday 12 December, 9am-1pm
Come and join Santa, make a free gift and see
who might visit!

To get involved, contact secretary@ramseyrotary.co.uk and book to attend the planning evening on Wednesday 11 November. Look out for the Santa Tracker to find out when he will visit your street.

Raising funds for the Mayor’s charities: Ramsey Rural Museum and the Armed Services Veterans Breakfast Club. No experience is needed - trust the process and you will have loads of fun and create a wonderful item. Click the QR code to book or email events@ramseytowncouncil.gov.uk . Events for you to come along and enjoy Scan the QR code to donate. Every pound is very much appreciated. Ramsey Christmas Lights is putting the tree up on Saturday 14 November. Complete the festive trail to collect your bauble, decorate it and have it hung on the tree. That afternoon there will be a children’s Christmas Party, a chance to have a family photograph taken by a professional photographer, Santa in his grotto for a selfie and a Snow Globe. The party is free and will be held at Ramsey Community Centre, with refreshments on sale. Switch-On Day - Saturday 28 November. The morning starts at 10am at Abbey College with the Christmas Bazaar. The town-centre switch-on starts at 3pm with a Taylor Swift tribute, and the lights go on at 5.15pm. The fairground will be in town until 8pm. There is an envelope with this newsletter, or you can scan the QR code above. news.content: Autumn 2026 Ramsey Town Council Residents Communication RAMSEY COMMUNITIES NEIGHBOURHOOD PLAN A further step forward The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan has been prepared with local voices at the heart. People gave their opinions via consultation over the summer of 2025 and the plan was then put together by a steering group of residents before going back out as a draft for further consultation. We’re pleased to say that it has also passed another significant step - Independent Assessment. Further details can be found on the Ramsey Town Council website. What happens next? The next major step will be a community vote through a referendum organised by Huntingdonshire District Council, likely to be in December 2026. It will be organised in the same way as an election and everyone on the electoral register will be notified. You will be asked whether you accept the Neighbourhood Plan - yes or no. We will produce a quick reference guide for anyone who may not have time to read the full document. Key points include: Providing new infrastructure, facilities and services so new development benefits existing, new and future residents. Supporting a vibrant community with places to live, work, stay and play, including affordable housing and housing with a local connection. Protecting the historic environment, heritage assets and green spaces that matter to the community. Having our Neighbourhood Plan in place will mean Ramsey receives 25% of developer contributions rather than the current 15%. That means more money can be spent directly in our community. neighbourhood.plan@ramseytowncouncil.gov.uk

news.content: CIL - Community Infrastructure Levy What is CIL? Community Infrastructure Levy, commonly referred to as CIL, is money collected by Huntingdonshire District Council from certain new developments. The funding is then used to help provide or improve infrastructure needed as communities grow. The money collected is broadly divided into three areas: Up to 5% can be retained by Huntingdonshire District Council towards the administration and collection of CIL. 15% is normally allocated to the Town or Parish Council for the area where the development takes place. Once an adopted Neighbourhood Plan is in place, this increases to 25%. Most of the remaining funding is retained by Huntingdonshire District Council for larger strategic infrastructure projects across the district. Ramsey Town Council currently receives the 15% neighbourhood portion. Once the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan is adopted, this will increase to 25%, giving the Council a greater share of money from qualifying development to invest back into our communities. Current projects supported or earmarked through Ramsey Town Council’s CIL funding include: Improvements at The Moorings. Contributions towards Local Highways Improvement projects. Improvements to Newtown Road Play Park. Improvements to the public toilets. New benches at the skate park. CCTV at The Moorings and New Road. The Double Yellow Lines project. The Town Council is also considering future projects, including additional parking behind the doctor’s surgery at Mews Close. Local Highways Initiative Bid (LHI): what is an LHI? The Local Highway Improvement programme allows local councils and community organisations to apply to Cambridgeshire County Council for funding towards highway improvements. Projects can include new or extended footpaths, traffic-calming measures, speed-reduction schemes, and other changes designed to improve road and pedestrian safety. Ramsey Town Council identifies potential projects and submits applications to Cambridgeshire County Council. Applications are assessed by the County Council and, if successful, funding is awarded towards the cost of the scheme. Under the current scheme, up to £25,000 can be awarded towards more complex projects, with applicants expected to contribute at least 10% of the overall cost. One recent LHI project was the extension of the footpath along Stocking Fen Road towards the industrial estate, improving pedestrian access for people travelling to and from work. The Council has also submitted an application for speed-reduction measures on the approach to Ramsey St Mary’s and is awaiting the outcome. Abbey College Road Safety Campaign Abbey College students are raising funds towards the £10,000 needed to help pay for speed reduction measures on Hollow Lane. Students have been campaigning, the school submitted an LHI bid, and speed cushions are planned. They would be grateful if you could spare the price of a coffee and scan the QR code.

UNANIMOUSLY for the Huntingdonshire District Council to APPROVE the application subject to 
the Highways concerns being satisfied. 
1.2 . 26/01440/FUL Change of use to a SEN day school (Class F1), erection of a rear single 
storey extension, external alterations to existing two-storey rear extension, and 
associated works including additional car parking, new landscaping, and recreation areas, 
Westward House, Bury Road, Ramsey, Huntingdon PE26 1NA Proposed by Cllr S Fice 
and seconded by Cllr L Knight Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for the 
District Council to APPROVE the application. They noted that Highways were now 
approving the application and the placement of the MUGA would  mitigate some of the 
noise concerns from residents. 
1.3 26/01526/FUL Temporary permission for a period of 15 years for the erection of 3 units for use as 
retail or community space and associated public realm and highway improvements – Pedestrian 
Island, Great Whyte, Ramsey. This item is on the agenda to complete the vote on the substantive 
motion on 1.1 from the meeting of 8
th
 October. The substantive motion is ‘There is insufficient 
information for Ramsey Town Council to be able to support the application.’ If this vote is 
defeated it will return to the original motion ‘To accept the application’ Cllr V Fendley explained 
to members that due to the substantive motion not being voted on at the previous meeting the vote 
would now be taken. After a discussion of understanding further information had been received 
since the last meeting and that Highways had also submitted their comments since the last 
meeting the vote was taken. 
 Cllr M Clarke asked for a recorded vote, Proposed by Cllr M Clarke and seconded by Cllr S Corney 
Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for a recorded vote to be taken. There was insufficient 
information for Ramsey Town Council to be able to support the application voting FOR Cllrs L 
Knight, M Clarke and J Clarke. AGAINST Cllrs V Fendley, S Corney E Welsh, J Bufton, S Fice, I 
Axelsen, A Costello, J Thompson and L Webster. This motion was defeated. The original motion was 
then discussed ‘To Accept the Planning Application’ Further discussion took place and Cllr S Fice 
proposed an amendment to the motion ‘To accept the Planning Application with the caveat that 

the Highways concerns are addressed.’ This was seconded by Cllr L Webster. Ramsey Town 
Council voted 9 FOR and 3 ABSTENTIONS for this motion to become the substantive motion. 
The vote on the substantive motion was then taken ‘To accept the Planning Application with the 
caveat that the Highways concerns are addressed.’ Proposed by Cllr S Fice and seconded by Cllr L 
Webster Ramsey Town Council voted 9 FOR and 3 ABSTENTIONS to accept the Planning Application 
with the caveat that the Highways concerns were addressed 
     340. Planning – other business 
a) Feedback about the online Planning Training hosted by Huntingdonshire District Council. 
Members felt it was very monotone and difficult for new members to follow. The training given 
on new members councillor training was much more informative. 
b) Feedback on the Development Management Committee reference the David Wilson Homes. 
Cllr S Corney feedback on the meeting where the Members at the Development Committee 
(DMC) voted to Refuse the 199 houses Land South of the Maltings, Ramsey. The hearing of 
the application took over 3.5 hours and between Ramsey Town Council, Bury PC and Sarah 
Harrington (representing residents) gave comprehensive reasons why the application should 
be refused. Whilst this was a success, the application will now be taken to the Secretary of 
State. Cllr S Corney then proposed that Ramsey Town Council seek planning advice about the 
David Wilson applications that were being developed and heard in smaller phases to stop the 
developer paying a larger sum for the Community Infrastructure Levy. The amount was 
thought to be approx. £6 million pounds the community had missed out on. At the DMC 
meeting which was recorded, the Agent for David Wilson Homes said he had been working 
with Huntingdonshire District Council for over two and a half years on the application. Cllr S 
Corney proposed to seek advice on this point. Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by 
Cllr J Clarke Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for Ramsey Town Council to seek 
planning advice on the cumulative effect on the David Wilson applications. 
c) To agree the representations to be submitted to Huntingdonshire District Council in 
response to their Local Plan consultation (previously circulated) Cllr V Fendley 
reminded the members the points in the document. Proposed by Cllr L Knight and 
seconded by Cllr S Corney Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY to accept 
the document to be submitted to Huntingdonshire District Council in response to their 
Local Plan. 
341. Meeting Dates 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council would take place on Thursday 12th November at 7pm.

metadata.title: Timeline of events after knifeman guilty of attempted murder on Huntingdon train
metadata.contentSnippet: Anthony Williams was found guilty of 14 attempted murders after a knife attack on an LNER train near Huntingdon on November 1, 2025.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Timeline of events after knifeman guilty of attempted murder on Huntingdon train
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An LNER service travelling from Doncaster to London King's Cross had just departed from Peterborough at around 7.30pm on November 1, 2025, when an unprecedented disaster struck. Emergency calls began flooding in to police, with passengers claiming a knife attack was taking place on board. Just 15 minutes after it left Peterborough, the train made an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon station after the driver took action and moved it onto the slower line. Anthony Williams, 33, was arrested at the scene and later charged with 14 counts of attempted murder, ten of which relate to the incident on the train. He pleaded guilty to wounding with intent and a handful of other offences including affray and common assault, but denied attempted murder. At Cambridge Crown Court on November 26, 2026, a jury of nine men and three women found him guilty of all 14 counts after a month-long trial. Below is a timeline of the events leading up to and during the attack, as set out by prosecutors during the trial. Around 7pm: Williams stabs a 14-year-old boy on a footbridge over the River Nene in Peterborough. The boy and his friend manage to escape. Minutes later: Williams encounters Dawid Taborski, 26, on the same bridge and attempts to stab him, but he flees. Soon after he encounters William Ogelby, 22, in the Rail World car park and his jacket is cut. Around 7.20pm: Williams arrives at Ritzy Barbers in Peterborough. He is caught on CCTV brandishing a knife and shouting, before leaving in a taxi. Williams in the Ritzy Barbers shop (Image: PA) 8.17pm: Williams arrives at Peterborough train station and boards a train to London. A passenger sends a text message to British Transport Police soon after informing them a man is acting suspiciously. Officers stop the train at Stevenage but cannot locate the man. 10.30pm: Williams is caught on CCTV stealing a set of kitchen knives from an Asda store in Stevenage. Soon after he boards another train to London. 11.30pm: Williams arrives at Farringdon station. 12.43am: Williams stabs 17-year-old Isaiah Idris on a DLR train heading to Pontoon Dock station. He gets off at Pontoon Dock before travelling around London on the Tube network and getting a train back to Stevenage. Williams on the DLR train (Image: BTP/Press Association) Around 6am: Williams steals alcohol from the same Stevenage Asda store. He then boards another train and gets off at Hitchin. Williams boarding a Thameslink train at Stevenage (Image: BTP/Press Association) 7.51am: Williams boards a train to Peterborough. On this service, he spits at passenger Jordan Morley, who gets off at Biggleswade. 9.30am: Williams arrives at his home address in Peterborough. He spends around nine hours here and makes a call to his bank. 7.26pm: Williams boards the LNER service to London King's cross which departs a few minutes later. 7.38pm: Police receive the first calls about a knife attack on board the train. Ten men were stabbed: LNER staff member Samir Zitouni, 48, and passengers Jonathan Gjoshe, 22, Sachin Balakrishnan, 29, David Presland, 73, Scott Bletcher, 50, Scott Green, 52, Kevin Deely, 58, Stephen Crean, 61, Raza Aslam, 44, and Michael Paffett, 34. Williams brandishing a knife on the LNER service (Image: BTP/Press Association) 7.44pm: The service makes an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon station. Armed police attend and Williams is arrested minutes later. 9.42pm: Williams arrives at Parkside Police Station in Cambridge. 3.27am: Williams punches police constable James Farrell on the nose while in custody.

metadata.title: The 'hidden gem' pub in Cambridgeshire that offers 'amazing' meals
metadata.contentSnippet: A quayside pub in Cambridgeshire has been described as a "hidden gem" and serves "amazing" meals, according to happy visitors.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The 'hidden gem' pub in Cambridgeshire that offers 'amazing' meals
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A quayside pub in Cambridgeshire has been described as a "hidden gem" and serves "amazing" meals, according to happy visitors. The Oliver Cromwell pub, on Wellington Street, St Ives, is nestled in a "characterful" Grade-II property near to the River Great Ouse. Its become a favourite of both locals and visitors for its fresh, seasonal menu and warm, friendly service. On Trip Advisor, the Cambridgeshire pub has more than 150 'excellent'-rated reviews, earning praise for its service and value. Elsewhere, on Google Reviews, The Oliver Cromwell has a score of 4.5 out of 5 from more than 600 reviews. The Oliver Cromwell, renowned for its excellent food, was forced to close its kitchen in July 2024, but soon reopened. It was taken over by Tom Blestoe who transformed it into a "traditional English pub", creating an environment where "where everyone can feel welcome". The menu "celebrates the best of British pub fare, with a focus on "fresh, locally-sourced ingredients prepared entirely in house." Guests can expect generous portions, seasonal specials and "a warm welcome waiting". Its dishes are complimented by a "strong selection" of cask ales, making it a "hit with diners and drinkers alike, the pub boats on its website. It is unsurprising, then, that The Oliver Cromwell has received rave reviews with guests praising its "excellent lunch" and live music. One visitor said: "Amazing food and service. We had a sandwich and loaded fries. Perfect sized portions and delicious food. "Staff really accommodating and friendly. Would definitely recommend." Another added: "Good Sunday lunches are few and far between. But the Oliver Cromwell is a MUST. Everything fantastic. No more words other than. Epic." "Really good lunch at this recently refurbished pub. Under new management with excellent staff. Also very reasonably priced. Will definitely return," another guest said. What's your favourite pub in Cambridgeshire? Let us know in the comments. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire woman’s weekly home help leads to lasting friendship
metadata.contentSnippet: A helping hand at home has led to a lasting friendship for one Cambridgeshire resident.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire woman’s weekly home help leads to lasting friendship
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A helping hand at home has led to a lasting friendship for one Cambridgeshire resident. Louise, who lives in Cambridgeshire, was recovering from a fall down the stairs in March while already managing arthritis and fatigue from her medication. She was unable to manage daily tasks and became isolated during her recovery, with her sons out at work and college during the day and limited mobility keeping her indoors. Louise said: "I was very lonely after the accident. "There was somebody that would come in regularly once a week, just to do even the lightest bit of housework. "It just made such a difference because I couldn't do anything." On a friend’s recommendation, she contacted Care Network Cambridgeshire and was matched with volunteer Sandra through the charity’s Help at Home service. Sandra visited weekly for approximately two months, helping with light household tasks, benefits paperwork, and personal difficulties, while also offering reassurance and practical guidance. The support soon grew into a friendship, and the two remain in touch even after formal support ended. Louise said: "I ended up with one of the ladies who, even after I was discharged from Care Network, has now become a firm friend. "It was just so lovely knowing that there was somebody there who cared about us." Lynda Phillips, CEO of Care Network Cambridgeshire, said: "Louise's story shows that sometimes it's the simplest things that make the biggest difference. "Having someone come into your home, help with everyday tasks and take the time to listen can mean so much when you're feeling isolated or struggling." The charity, which marked its 40th anniversary in October 2026, is encouraging more people to volunteer or support its work to help others facing similar challenges. For more information on volunteering, accessing support, or making a donation, visit www.care-network.org.uk.

metadata.title: St Neots veterans share stories and support at Huntingdon afternoon tea
metadata.contentSnippet: St Neots Royal Naval Association veterans joined former service personnel for a Veterans’ Afternoon Tea at The Chase Care Home in Huntingdon on November 21.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Neots veterans share stories and support at Huntingdon afternoon tea
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Veterans from the St Neots branch of the Royal Naval Association joined residents and former service personnel for a special afternoon tea at The Chase Care Home in Huntingdon. The Chase Care Home hosted the November 21 afternoon tea, giving veterans a chance to share their experiences and chat. The event brought veterans from different services together in friendship and mutual understanding. Friendship - Veterans came together to share stories of their time in the military (Image: Simon Cartwright) The conversation covered funny anecdotes, tales of adventure, military service and life after the forces. The veterans found common ground through their shared experiences in uniform, even though some had never met before. Staff at The Chase Care Home were praised for their care and support, which helped create a welcoming atmosphere for conversation and friendship. Delicious - the cream tea offered at the event (Image: Simon Cartwright) Events like this help veterans talk openly about their experiences, tackle isolation and make new friends. The return of a Royal Navy Vanguard-class submarine after a 217-day Continuous At Sea Deterrent patrol has underlined the importance of these connections. Such deployments place significant demands on those serving and their families, emphasising the need for veterans and serving personnel to have opportunities to talk, reflect, and support one another. A member who served 23 years as an engineer in the Royal Navy Submarine Service highlighted the value of shared understanding among veterans. The St Neots branch says even a simple conversation can make a real difference to veterans. Speaking openly with fellow veterans can bring reassurance, perspective and strength in good times and bad. The Veterans' Afternoon Tea at The Chase Care Home captured the Royal Naval Association’s spirit of friendship, mutual support and lifelong comradeship. The St Neots Branch expressed its gratitude to Gemma Keech and all the staff at The Chase Care Home for their hospitality and looks forward to supporting similar events in the future. The branch stressed the importance of conversation among veterans. The event showed the enduring strength of the Armed Forces family and the importance of keeping veterans connected.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Royal Mail has issued a fresh warning for potential delivery delays across postcodes in Cambridgeshire. The postal service has published a list of 29 postcode areas across the UK that could be impacted on Friday (November 27). In a statement, Royal Mail said: "We aim to deliver to all addresses we have mail for, six days a week. "In a small number of local offices, this may temporarily not be possible due to local issues such as high levels of sick absence, resourcing, or other local factors. "In those cases, we will rotate deliveries to minimise the delay to individual customers. "We also provide targeted support to those offices to address their challenges and restore our service to the high standard our customers would normally receive." It added: "We're sorry for any inconvenience and thank you for your understanding." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Further details have emerged after a reported trespass incident caused disruption to rail services in Cambridgeshire. National Rail first confirmed "trespassers on the railway" at Cambridge at around 5pm on Thursday (November 27). It added all lines were blocked, with trains calling at Cambridge railway station delayed by up to 30 minutes or revised as a result. However, all lines reopened at around 5.30pm and services returned to normal, with disruption expected until 6.45pm. In an update on Friday (November 27), the British Transport Police confirmed it was called to reports of a trespasser on the tracks at Cambridge. A spokesperson said: "Officers responded and searched the area thoroughly, however no one was found." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Huntingdon bed factory’s £1m relaunch keeps British craftsmanship alive
metadata.contentSnippet: A bed factory that has been making mattresses for more than 60 years is keeping traditional craftsmanship alive.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon bed factory’s £1m relaunch keeps British craftsmanship alive
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A bed factory that has been making mattresses for more than 60 years is keeping traditional craftsmanship alive. Generations of families have worked at Bensons for Beds’ Huntingdon site, where craftsmen still use hand side-stitching and tufting every day. The factory, which opened in 1962, is now playing a key role in the relaunch of heritage bed brand Staples & Co, first established in 1895. One of the team at work in the factory. (Image: Rosie Pratt) Nick Collard, chief executive officer of Bensons for Beds, said: "What makes our Huntingdon factory special isn't just what we make here. "It's the people, the pride they take in their work and the knowledge that has been built up over decades. "There are families whose connections to bedmaking in Huntingdon stretch back generations. "That's an extraordinary legacy, and one we have a responsibility to protect." the skilled craftspeople at Bensons for Beds' Cambridgeshire manufacturing facility are playing a central role in the relaunch of Staples & Co, a historic British bed brand founded in 1895, following an investment of more than £1 million.  (Image: Rosie Pratt) The relaunch follows an investment of more than £1 million by Bensons for Beds and aims to combine modern manufacturing with traditional British craftsmanship. The refreshed Staples & Co collection features contemporary designs and high-quality natural materials, including regeneratively farmed British wool. The Huntingdon team, which includes employees with more than 40 years of experience, is now training a new generation of apprentices to carry the skills forward. Inspecting the quality of a mattress. (Image: Rosie Pratt) Mr Collard said: "At the same time, we want to create opportunities for young people to build rewarding careers in manufacturing. "The future of British bedmaking depends on passing that expertise on, while giving the next generation the opportunity to develop skills of their own." Bensons for Beds supports apprenticeships and specialist training programmes at the site, aiming to secure the long-term future of the craft. One of the team tape edging a mattress in the Staples factory. (Image: Rosie Pratt) The Huntingdon factory is central to the company’s UK operations, combining traditional methods with innovation and large-scale production. It also holds the Furniture Makers' Manufacturing Guild Mark and BSI Kitemark, reflecting its production standards. Bensons for Beds owned brands director Emma Forbes said: "There's something remarkable about watching a skilled bedmaker at work. One of the team tape edging a mattress in the Staples factory. (Image: Rosie Pratt) "Techniques such as hand side-stitching take time to master, and you can see the care and precision that goes into every stage. "When we developed the new Staples & Co collection, we wanted to create products that genuinely benefit from that expertise. "It's about the details you may not immediately see, but which make a real difference to how a mattress feels and performs." One of the team at work in the factory. (Image: Rosie Pratt) "Being able to draw on the skills and experience of our Huntingdon team is a real strength for the brand." She said the Huntingdon team’s experience and skill are a "real strength" for the brand. The Staples & Co relaunch is part of Bensons’ wider growth plan, which includes investing in its brands and UK manufacturing. One of the team tape edging a mattress. (Image: Rosie Pratt) The new collection will go on sale in Bensons stores nationwide from November. The Huntingdon site has employed several generations of the same families, underlining its deep community roots. It makes Bensons for Beds mattresses, including Staples & Co ranges, using specialist techniques and natural materials. The skilled craftspeople at Bensons for Beds' Cambridgeshire manufacturing facility are playing a central role in the relaunch of Staples & Co, a historic British bed brand founded in 1895, following an investment of more than £1 million.  (Image: Rosie Pratt) The factory also supports apprenticeships and ongoing training to build its skilled workforce. Staples & Co is a heritage brand founded in 1895 and now owned by Bensons for Beds. Backed by an investment of more than £1 million, the relaunch combines traditional craft with modern design across three mattress ranges – Artisan, Signature and Iconic – plus matching divan bases and headboards. One of the team at work in the factory. (Image: Rosie Pratt) Selected collections use regeneratively farmed British wool sourced from a network of approximately 50 to 60 farmers. Bensons for Beds calls itself the UK’s leading sleep specialist, with more than 175 stores and a focus on personalised service and quality products. The factory in Huntingdon. (Image: Rosie Pratt) The company employs over 1,700 people across its retail, manufacturing and distribution operations.

metadata.title: Waste management firm shares update on cause of huge building fire
metadata.contentSnippet: The operator of a waste management building which caught fire in St Neots has issued an update on the cause of the blaze.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Waste management firm shares update on cause of huge building fire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The operator of a waste management building which caught fire has issued an update on the cause of the blaze. Firefighters from across Cambridgeshire rushed to the Biffa Waste Management Transfer Station on Marston Road, Eynesbury, St Neots, on August 11. Crews from Wisbech, March, Chatteris, Yaxley, Cambridge, Sawtry, Littleport and St Neots alongside a crew from Bedfordshire attended. An eyewitness described the blaze as a "tower of smoke" (Image: Leon Rawson) Crews tackled the blaze wearing breathing apparatus and using hose reels to bring the fire under control. Members of the public living nearby were advised to keep windows and doors closed due to smoke in the area. An eyewitness at the scene described the blaze as "a tower of smoke", with others reporting the fire could be seen from a long way away. Firefighters remained at the scene for several days (Image: Newsquest) Crews remained at the scene for several days, carrying out regular inspections to identify hot spots and prevent further spread. In a statement released weeks after the blaze, Biffa said the fire involved a "steel framed building containing dry mixed recycling". This included "cardboard, cans and bottles, together with general waste, collected from local businesses." In an update on Friday (November 27), the waste management firm confirmed an investigation was "unable to formally confirm the cause of the fire". Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: Drug dealer jailed for supplying crack cocaine and heroin in Cambridgeshire
metadata.contentSnippet: Peterborough drug dealer Curtis Reeve jailed for 47 months after admitting supplying crack cocaine and heroin, with police uncovering cash and designer goods.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drug dealer jailed for supplying crack cocaine and heroin in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A drug dealer has been jailed for running a crack cocaine and heroin supply operation in Cambridgshire. Curtis Reeve, 27, was arrested on January 6 after police executed a warrant at his home on Cobden Avenue in Millfield, Peterborough. Officers found a mobile phone linked to a drug line and several wraps of crack cocaine. A police investigation uncovered hundreds of calls and messages with other dealers, including texts detailing drug quantities and evidence of topped-up phones connected to the operation. Reeve was also found with more than £2,000 in cash and evidence he had purchased designer goods worth £1,600, despite being unemployed and claiming benefits. The items included a pair of Dolce and Gabbana trainers worth £579 and a Moncler coat costing £659. He purchased a pair of Dolce and Gabbana trainers worth £579 (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) He purchased a Moncler coat costing £659 (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Other suspected dealers arrested with large amounts of class A drugs were also found to have links to Reeve through their mobile phones. He admitted being concerned in the supply of crack cocaine and heroin, as well as possessing criminal property. On November 24, he was sentenced to 47 months in prison at Cambridge Crown Court. Curtis Reeve was jailed for 47 months (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Detective Constable James Campbell said: "This investigation showed Reeve was a significant member of an organised crime group supplying crack cocaine and heroin. "He tried to distance himself from the operation by getting others to hold most of the drugs and complete the dealing, but the evidence of his involvement was clear. "Class A drug dealers trade in human misery – whether that be those exploited as part of the operation or those trapped in addiction. "We will continue to do all we can to identify people involved in supplying drugs in Cambridgeshire and bring them before the courts." For information concerning the signs of drug dealing, or to report information, visit Cambridgeshire Constabulary's website.

Check your change as rare Royal Mint 20p coin sells for 1,800 times face value
metadata.contentSnippet: The 20p piece is a “mule” coin dating from 2008 and was minted without a date on the coin due to an error.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Check your change as rare Royal Mint 20p coin sells for 1,800 times face value
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: We are all being encouraged to check our change after a rare 20p coin sold for more than 1,800 times its face value this week. The 20p piece is a “mule” coin dating from 2008 and was minted without a date on the coin due to an error. The mistake means the coin is considered a collector’s item. A batch of coins was issued without dates in 2008 due to an error in the minting process. An example of a rare undated 20p mule coin  (Image: eBay/Getty/Vandervelden) Prior to November of that year, the date on 20p coins would be found on the tail side. However, the Royal Mint switched it so that the date would now be next to the Queen’s head. A mistake in 2008 led to the old format being used on the Queen’s side and the new format being used on tails side. As a result, the first batch of British coins with no date on them was released into circulation for the first time in more than 300 years. Around 250,000 20p coins minted in November 2008 are believed to have entered circulation with no date. And now one has sold on eBay, attracting a winning bid of £363, 1,815 times its face value. The 50 pence piece has become the most valued and collected coin in the UK, with many collectable designs appearing on its heptagonal canvas. Its 27.5mm diameter makes it the largest of any British coin, and allows space for decorative pictures. It has often been used to celebrate big events over the past 50 years of British history. The rarest coins tend to be of the greatest value, with the mintage (number of coins with each design made) being the fundamental attraction for collectors. Along with the design, other aspects of the coin which increase value are the condition of the coin and whether it has an error in its design. The way in which it is sold can also determine the coin’s value - while some coin collectors will bid vast amounts of money on eBay or at auction, others opt for more robust valuations by selling via a coin dealer.

metadata.title: Martin Lewis slams 'ridiculous' energy-saving advice as bills rocket this winter
metadata.contentSnippet: Martin Lewis has hit out at the “ridiculous” tips households are having to follow to keep warm, saying it is not the kind of society he wants to live in.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis slams 'ridiculous' energy-saving advice as bills rocket this winter
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Lewis has hit out at the “ridiculous” tips households are having to follow to keep warm and cut their energy bills, saying it is not the kind of society he wants to live in. The Money Saving Expert founder said people were being forced to rely on basic energy-saving measures and even USB-heated clothing to stay warm as the cost of heating their homes continues to put pressure on household budgets. Speaking to the BBC, Martin reluctantly said households should first look at ways to reduce energy use without affecting their quality of life. He advised people to keep curtains closed when it is dark and open during daylight, make sure blinds face inwards and avoid hanging curtains over radiators. He also urged households to check their radiators are properly bled and, if they have a combi boiler, look at whether its flow temperature is set too high. But Martin said the fact people need this kind of advice in order to manage their heating costs was a sign of a much wider problem. “Again, I don't, you know, it's not because we want to live in that society, but we do live in that society. It's ridiculous,” he said. He also pointed to 1p an hour USB-heated clothing as another way people are trying to keep themselves warm without having to heat their entire home. “The USB heated gilet costs a penny an hour to run. It keeps you warm. It doesn't keep your house warm, but it'll keep you going,” he said. Martin added: “And we are in that situation, and that's not a society I want to live in, where we have to be giving out that type of information and advice. But it is there, and it is going to be happening.” Recommended reading : His comments underline the pressure facing households as they look for ways to keep energy costs down, with simple changes around the home being presented as ways to make heating go further.

metadata.title: Knifeman guilty of attempted murder on train forced to stop in Huntingdon
metadata.contentSnippet: Anthony Williams found guilty of seven counts of attempted murder after a LNER train attack near Huntingdon on November 1, with verdicts pending on seven further charges.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Knifeman guilty of attempted murder on train forced to stop in Huntingdon
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A knifeman who wounded several people on a train which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon has been found guilty of seven counts of attempted murder. Several people were injured on the LNER train from Doncaster to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025. Anthony Williams, 33, denied 14 counts of attempted murder: ten of them in relation to the LNER train, three said to have happened in Peterborough and one at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London. He previously pleaded guilty to wounding with intent, as well as affray, common assault and a number of other charges. At Cambridge Crown Court on November 26, a jury of nine men and three women found Williams guilty of seven counts of attempted murder. Williams is guilty of the attempted murders of LNER staff member Samir Zitouni and six passengers on the train: Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, and Stephen Crean. The jury has yet to reach a verdict on the remaining seven counts of attempted murder. The judge, Mr Justice Calver, said he would accept a majority, of 11 or 10 of the 12 jurors, on the remaining seven counts.

metadata.title: Knifeman guilty of all 14 counts of attempted murder after Huntingdon train attack
metadata.contentSnippet: Anthony Williams, who stabbed ten people on a train which was forced to stop in Huntingdon, has been found guilty of all 14 counts of attempted murder.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Knifeman guilty of all 14 counts of attempted murder after Huntingdon train attack
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A knifeman who stabbed ten people on a train which was forced to stop in Cambridgeshire has been found guilty of all 14 counts of attempted murder. Several people were injured on the LNER train from Doncaster to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025, which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon. Anthony Williams, 33, denied 14 counts of attempted murder: ten of them in relation to the LNER train, three said to have happened in Peterborough and one at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London. He pleaded guilty to wounding with intent, as well as affray, common assault and a number of other charges. After a month-long trial, a jury of nine men and three women found him guilty of all 14 counts of attempted murder at Cambridge Crown Court on November 26. The court was shown CCTV footage (Image: PA) The incidents concern a 14-year-old boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, that Williams stabbed on a footbridge over the River Nene in Peterborough at around 7pm on October 31, 2025. Shortly afterwards, he attempted to stab Dawid Taborski, then 26, and then William Ogelby, 22, in the Rail World car park. After travelling to London by train, Williams stabbed Isaiah Idris, then 17, on a DLR train travelling to Pontoon Dock station at around 12.40am on November 1. Anthony Williams boarding a Thameslink train at Stevenage station (Image: BTP/Press Association) He travelled back to Peterborough by train and boarded the LNER service to London King's Cross at 7.29pm. Williams is guilty of attempting to murder LNER staff member Samir Zitouni and passengers Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, Stephen Crean, Kevin Deely, Raza Aslam and Michael Paffett on board the train. The train was scheduled to next stop at Stevenage, but was forced to make an emergency stop at Huntingdon at 7.44pm after the driver was alerted to what was going on. Williams was arrested minutes later.

metadata.title: 'Low-quality CCTV' delayed identification of Hunts train stabber by 18 hours
metadata.contentSnippet: Police took 18 hours to identify Anthony Williams after a DLR knife attack on Isaiah Idris, with British Transport Police blaming low-quality CCTV in London.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Low-quality CCTV' delayed identification of Hunts train stabber by 18 hours
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police took 18 hours to identify Anthony Williams as a suspect in a knife attack because of “low-quality” CCTV, an officer said. British Transport Police defended their handling of the attack on Isaiah Idris, now 18, who Williams knifed on a Docklands Light Railway train approaching Pontoon Dock in London. Williams asked the teenager “are you beefing with the devil?” before slashing his face at about 12.43am on November 1, 2025. CCTV of Williams on the DLR (Image: BTP/Press Association) Williams, 33, was identified as a suspect at 2.52pm, 14 hours later. Officers found he was registered to two addresses. Four hours later, officers reached Waltham Cross in Hertfordshire but found they had gone to the wrong address. By the time officers reached Waltham Cross, Williams had left his Peterborough address and was less than an hour from attacking a packed LNER train. Detective Superintendent Sam Blackburn, of British Transport Police’s Major, Serious and Organised Crime Unit, would not say whether police missed chances to stop Williams before the LNER attack. He said “low-quality CCTV” had hampered efforts to identify the knifeman who stabbed Mr Idris. “The insufficient quality of the CCTV on board that (DLR) train and at Pontoon Dock meant we couldn’t identify Anthony Williams maybe as quickly as we’d like,” said Mr Blackburn. (Image: PA) He said officers began planning Williams’s arrest once they identified him as the suspect. “There were two addresses we could have gone to,” Mr Blackburn said. “Those two addresses were Waltham Cross (in Hertfordshire) and Peterborough (in Cambridgeshire). “Intelligence supported our attendance first at the Waltham Cross address because it’s closer to Pontoon Dock, which is a factor. “But also the intelligence supported us through financial checks on Anthony Williams which linked him to that Waltham Cross address.” He said officers reached the Waltham Cross address at about 6.45pm on November 1, 2025. Mr Blackburn said it was “important to note” Williams had “left his home address in Peterborough” at 6.15pm that evening. “So even if we’d gone to a Peterborough address, we chose the Waltham Cross address, either address Mr Williams wouldn’t have been present,” he said. The officer continued: “By the time we’ve carried out our inquiry at the Waltham Cross address the Huntingdon attack has already happened.” The LNER train left Peterborough at about 7.29pm and made an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon at 7.44pm after Williams attacked. Mr Blackburn said Williams had boarded a DLR service at West Silvertown in London before the attack on Mr Idris. “On boarding that service the doors have shut and Mr Williams has almost immediately attacked a 17-year-old boy called Isaiah Idris,” he said. “Isaiah was seriously injured. “It’s not violence we normally see on the network and so we responded accordingly. “We responded within 10 minutes, us and other emergency services partners, to that incident and we began that serious investigation of trying to obtain evidence that was available to us.” An officer has explained why police took 18 hours to identify the train stabbing suspect (Image: PA) Mr Blackburn said the initial “CCTV harvesting wasn’t successful”. “But we looked at widening that search within those early hours, extending that search to other stations utilising our partners within TfL (Transport for London) and eventually we managed to obtain an image of the individual at Poplar, a completely different station to where the offence took place,” he said. “It was using that image that we then managed to identify Anthony Williams.” He described the response to Mr Idris’s attack as “proportionate and professional”. “We did everything we could to identify Williams as soon as we possibly could with the information that we had, with the CCTV that was available to us,” Mr Blackburn said. “It is difficult and I don’t want to speculate, but low-quality CCTV does limit us then in our ability to be able to identify individuals. “When we see the high-quality CCTV as we have seen on the LNER service itself and at other stations in London the process of identification becomes a lot easier.” On October 31, 2025, British Transport Police received a text report about a man “acting erratically and intoxicated” on a train travelling from Peterborough to Stevenage. The man was Williams, though this was not known at the time. Mr Blackburn said British Transport Police officers went to Stevenage station and “noticed the male who was on the tracks”. CCTV footage issued by British Transport Police showing Anthony Williams boarding a Thameslink train at Stevenage station (Image: BTP/Press Association) “Those were live tracks,” he said. “The officers have to consider their own safety and the safety of others. “They removed the power from the tracks and then conducted a full search to try and find that individual, a male we didn’t know at that stage was Anthony Williams. “Following that search it was a negative result but we did what we could in that instance in relation to responding to the information we were given.”

metadata.title: Huntingdon train stabbing: Audio of call between driver and signaller released
metadata.contentSnippet: New audio reveals LNER driver reported a knifeman after 10 people were stabbed on a London-bound train, which he stopped at Huntingdon on November 1.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon train stabbing: Audio of call between driver and signaller released
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The driver of a train on which 10 people were stabbed told a signaller he had “a report of a person with a knife on board” in newly released audio of a call between the two staff. Driver Andrew Johnson previously told jurors at Cambridge Crown Court that someone activated an alarm on the London-bound service and he heard “someone screaming ‘there’s a knifeman stabbing people’” over an intercom. Nine passengers and one member of on-board staff, Samir Zitouni, were stabbed by Anthony Williams during the attack on the high-speed service on November 1 last year. The LNER train, which had departed Peterborough at 7.29pm, was next scheduled to stop at Stevenage, with the journey due to take 30 minutes. Mr Johnson said in evidence that he decided to stop the service sooner at Huntingdon and “it just came instinctively, I never really thought about it”. The train made its unscheduled stop at Huntingdon at 7.44pm. He earlier told the trial that the service was travelling at 122mph around Abbots Ripton when an alarm went off “which indicated someone was trying to open one of the passenger doors”. He contacted a signaller after he heard over an intercom that there was a knifeman attacking people, and he heard a scream he described as “terrifying”. In newly released audio, Mr Johnson tells signaller Rob Pape: “Hello signaller… I’ve got an egress happened. I’ve got a report of a person with a knife on board. “I’m going to stop at Huntingdon.” The signaller tells Mr Johnson he will “get you in on the slow” line as the pair work to bring the train in safely. Mr Johnson asks Mr Pape: “Can you also inform police immediately?” The signaller replies: “Yes – so you’ve got a report of a passenger with a knife on board.” The driver says: “Yes, please”. The signaller says: “There’s a train in platform two at the moment, as soon as that departs, I’ll get you into platform two”. Mr Johnson replies: “Yes, and inform police immediately, thank you very much.” The driver said, in his evidence at trial: “My mind was completely focused on one thing and that was getting the train to Huntingdon.”

metadata.title: Co-op 'do not eat' warning issued as product recalled over health concerns
metadata.contentSnippet: Co-op is recalling 140g packs of king prawns after a labelling error gave them incorrect use-by dates. Check the affected dates and refund advice.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Co-op 'do not eat' warning issued as product recalled over health concerns
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Co-op is recalling king prawns after packs were labelled with the wrong use-by dates. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) said the affected prawns are unsafe to eat after their correct dates in November, despite the labels showing dates in December. The recall affects 140g packs of Co-op King Prawns in a Chilli & Coriander Marinade with printed use-by dates of December 27 and December 30. Packs marked December 27 should have a use-by date of November 27, while those marked December 30 should say November 30. Wednesday 25 November - Co-op recalls Co-op King Prawns in a Chilli & Coriander Marinade because of incorrect use by dates #FoodAlert https://t.co/4CSbgpyRMR https://t.co/msTp00x8su — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) November 25, 2026 The FSA said customers should not eat the product after the correct use-by date and can return it to a Co-op store for a refund or replacement, subject to availability. Co-op's customer notice separately tells shoppers to dispose of the product. In the notice, Co-op said: "For a refund or replacement (subject to availability) please visit your local store. "If purchased online, you can receive a refund by calling 0330 041 7737. "You can contact our Customer Careline on 0800 0686 727 or email via Product issues or returns - Co-op ( coop.co.uk ). "We apologise for any inconvenience caused." The FSA said notices explaining the recall and what customers should do will be displayed in stores selling the product. If a food product should not be sold because of a problem, it may be withdrawn from shelves or recalled, meaning customers are asked to return it. The FSA issues product recall information notices to inform consumers and local authorities about problems with food. In some cases, it issues a food alert for action, giving local authorities details of action to take on behalf of consumers.

See our full guide to food and drink advent calendars here. However, shoppers can still get their hands on the 12-day version, which is packed with 12 Liz Earle favourites and has a stated contents value of £203.50. The calendar includes: The offer is available online only while stocks last. Bimble & Bolt has two advent calendars designed to make December a little more active or relaxing. The Runners Advent Calendar, priced from £42, is packed with kit and treats to keep runners moving through the festive season. A new men's version is also being released for 2026. For those who prefer a slower pace, the Yoga & Wellness Advent Calendar costs £39.99 and offers 24 days of mindful treats and practical extras designed to support rest, recovery and everyday wellbeing. Together, they offer something a little different from the usual chocolate countdown. Price: Runners from £42; Yoga & Wellness £39.99, from Bimble & Bolt Best for: Collectables fans The Entertainer has a festive line-up of toy advent calendars for children, with 24 days of surprises from popular brands and characters. Options include LEGO Disney Princess, Star Wars and Marvel calendars, alongside KPop Demon Hunters, Squishmallows, One Piece and the Early Learning Centre Happyland calendar. Squishmallow advent calendar (Image: Squishmallow) There's also a quirky Squishy Dumpling option, with a mini squishy to discover behind each door. Prices start at £30, with calendars aimed at different age groups, from toddlers to older children. The Squishmallows calendar has already sold out during pre-sale, but is expected to return before December. Price: From £30, The Entertainer Best for: Luxury home fragrance lovers (Image: Chase and Wonder) Make the countdown to Christmas feel extra special with the Chase and Wonder Luxury Advent Calendar, which contains 12 individually wrapped gifts worth more than £430. Priced at £295, just 200 calendars will be available. The collection includes a showstopping ceramic candle made from fine bone china, hand-decorated with 22ct gold and handmade in Stoke-on-Trent. There are also six glass candles featuring the brand's best-loved fragrances, two room sprays, two travel tins and a jar of luxury matches. Everything comes presented in a newly designed keepsake box, making this a lavish treat for anyone who loves filling their home with beautiful scents. Price: £295, Chase and Wonder Best for: Little builders and creative children Magnatiles advent calendar (Image: Magnatiles) Give little ones something to build throughout December with the MAGNA-TILES Advent Calendar. Rather than 24 toys that might quickly be forgotten, each door reveals another piece to add to one big festive creation. Children will discover magnetic tiles, figures and accessories as they gradually build their own winter wonderland. The pieces are also compatible with the wider MAGNA-TILES range, meaning they can be mixed and matched with existing sets and enjoyed long after Christmas Day. Price: £39.99, Amazon Best for: Parents looking for a chocolate-free countdown Tonic vitamin advent calendar (Image: Tonic) Swap the usual chocolate for something different with Tonic's Kids' Vitamin Countdown Calendar. Priced at £25, it offers an alternative to the traditional advent calendar, with vitamin gummies and a daily activity behind its 25 doors. The gummies come from across Tonic's children's range, while the activities encourage little ones to move, draw, dance or do something kind. The idea is to make the countdown about more than just a daily sweet treat, giving children something fun to look forward to each morning. The Chilli No. 5 Hot Sauce & Spice Advent Calendar takes adventurous foodies on a spicy journey across the globe, starting in England and finishing in Africa, with the heat building behind every door. A seriously saucy Chilli No 5 Advent Calendar (Image: Chilli No 5) Inside are 24 gourmet surprises, from Wicked Wasabi and Jamaican Jerk Spice Rub to White Truffle Sauce, Carolina Reaper Flakes and Sriracha. The grand finale is a limited-edition 100ml bottle of Pure, combining Ghost, Scorpion and Reaper chillies. With 30 Great Taste Stars awarded to its products, it's a seriously hot gift for spice lovers. Recommended reading : Best for: Chilli enthusiasts, adventurous foodies and anyone who likes their Christmas with a fiery kick.
