Community Aspirations
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For the Theme – Heritage & Environment, the following are the community aspirations:
Heritage & Tourism

The parish is home to a wealth of heritage assets, and the historic environment has been identified through public consultation as being of particular importance to local residents. Specifically, it is a community aspiration to ensure that the heritage is adequately protected and supported. Events and assets such as the rural museum and Ramsey 1940s Camp are important both to the heritage of the area and the tourism offer.
Potential linkages to proposed major tourism provision at Bedford should be considered to see how the wider sub region can benefit from tourism investment and visitors.

In order to protect the heritage of the area, protection of areas like Stocking Fen and the area north  of  Tesco should  be  secured. Retaining  Ramsey  and  Bury  as distinct  settlements  is fundamental to the history of Ramsey; so, protecting a gap between Bury and Ramsey through maintaining a settlement break is a significant community aspiration.
The agricultural origins of the parish are a fundamental part of the character of the area. The preservation of agriculture and the agricultural heritage and culture is therefore important.
Great Fen & Biodiversity
The Great Fen project extends into Ramsey Heights and Ramsey St Mary’s, linkages to the Great Fen waterways plan and visitor centre is important.

The  biodiversity of  the  area and the protection  of  green  spaces is  important  to  allow  the communities  to enjoy  the  outside  for  recreation  and  views;  whilst  limiting  recreational disturbance to Woodwalton Fen which is a designated nature conservation site.
Protecting  and  enhancing  the rights  of  ways  and  paths would  contribute  to  the  health  and enjoyment of the local community.
The implications of flood risk should be considered in all aspects of life and development.

24. Natural Environment

24.1 Most  of  the parish  of Ramsey is rural  and contains  substantial  areas  of  farmland  which contributes  significantly  to  the  character  of  the parish  and  the  setting  of  the town  and villages.

24.2 There is a need to assess the likelihood of proposals or policies within a Neighbourhood Plan having a significant effect on the ‘National Sites Network’ consisting of areas designated as Special Areas of Conservation (SAC) or Special Protection Areas (SPA’s). Consideration of the internationally designated Ramsar sites is also necessary; many Ramsar sites are also SACs or  SPAs. In  the  vicinity  of the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area  the ‘National Sites Network’ of interest  are  the Orton  Pit  SAC  (Peterborough); Nene  Washes  SPA/Ramsar (East  of Peterborough);   Ouse   Washes   SAC/SPA/Ramsar (North-west   of   Ely);   Portholme   SAC (Huntingdon/Godmanchester); and Fenland SAC/Woodwalton Fen Ramsar.
24.3 The  closest  to  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area is  the Fenland  SAC/Woodwalton  Fen  Ramsar which immediately abuts the south-west corner of the parish near Ramsey Heights.

24.4 SACs  were  previously  classified  in  accordance  with  EC  Directive  92/43/EEC  on  the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora (the Habitats Directive). Article 3  of  this  Directive  requires  the  establishment  of  a  European  network  of  important high‐ quality  conservation  sites  that  will  make  a  significant  contribution  to  conserving  the  189 habitat types and 788 species identified in Annexes I and II of the Directive. These sites are now  designated  under  the  Conservation  of  Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  (as amended).

24.5 SPAs  were  sites  first  classified  in  accordance  with  Article  4  of  the  EC  Directive  on  the conservation of wild birds (79/409/EEC), more commonly known as the Birds Directive. They were classified for rare and vulnerable birds, listed in Annex I to the Birds Directive, and for regularly occurring migratory species. These SPA sites are now designated under the Wildlife
Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version)
60 &  Countryside  Act  1981  (as  amended)  and  the  Conservation  (Natural  Habitats,  &  c.) Regulations 2010 (as amended).

24.6 Ramsar Sites are designated under the International Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat (the Ramsar Convention, Iran 1971 and amended by  the  Paris  Protocol  1992).  Although Ramsar  Sites are not protected in law by domestic  UK  legislation  as  a  matter  of policy   government, has   decreed   that unless   otherwise   specified   procedures relating  to  SPAs  and  SACs  will  also  apply to Ramsar Sites.

24.7 The    Habitats    Regulation    Assessment screening identifies that the Neighbourhood  Plan  proposals  would  not individually  or  cumulatively  result  in  any potential    significant    effects    on    any designated site.

24.8 The plan area contains no National Nature Reserves (NNR), Woodwalton Fen is also a NNR in addition to being a SAC and Ramsar  site. The other nearest NNR are at Upwood Meadows around 2km to the south-west and Holme Fen around 2km to the west of Ramsey St Mary’s. The Plan area contains no Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs). Woodwalton Fen is also a SSSI in addition to being an NNR, SAC and Ramsar site; Holme Fen is also a SSSI as well as being an NNR. Warboys  and  Wistow  Woods  SSSI  lies around  3km  to  the  south  of  Ramsey (town).

24.9 There are impact zones defined around the various designated sites to identify what scale of different types of development need consultation with Natural England. This principally impacts  on  Ramsey  Heights  and  Ramsey  St  Mary’s,  although  the  impact  zones  do  extend further across the Parish. These impact zones are shown in Appendix 1.

24.10 In  terms  of County  level  locally  designated  sites (County  Wildlife  Sites),  the  plan  area contains Ramsey Heights Nature Reserve and Reservoir East of Park Farm which lies north- east of Ramsey towards Ramsey Hollow.

24.11 The Great Fen Project Area extends into the western part of the parish near Ramsey Heights and Ramsey St Mary’s. The Great Fen Landscape & Visual Setting boundary extends across the western part of the parish, covering land west of Ugg Mere Court Road in Ramsey Heights and west of the B1040 in Ramsey St Mary’s.

24.12 The Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS 44 ) is a bold new plan to revive and protect nature across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. It’s a locally driven, government-backed initiative that maps out where and how we can restore habitats, boost biodiversity, and reconnect people with the natural world, from countryside to city parks.

26.3 Fluvial (river) flooding and surface water flooding risks change over  time, in part at least due to the impact of climate change. Developers when designing surface water systems have to design them with an allowance for climate change 50 . During December 2020 there were a large volume of flood incidents across Cambridgeshire, Ramsey was affected. The Lead Local Flood Authority (LLFA) undertook a statutory flood investigation and produced the relevant report 51 .

26.4 SuDS   are   an   approach   to   managing surface  water  run-off  which  seeks  to mimic  natural  drainage  systems  and retain  water  on  or  near  the  site  as opposed     to     traditional     drainage approaches which involve piping water off  site  as  quickly  as  possible.  SuDS offer    significant    advantages    over conventional piped drainage systems in reducing  flood  risk  by  attenuating  the rate and quantity of surface water run- off from a site, promoting groundwater recharge, and improving water quality, biodiversity and amenity. The LLFA would particularly support above-ground open SuDS such as wetlands, attenuation basins, ponds and swales as they provide additional amenity and biodiversity benefits.

26.5 Opportunities for increasing biodiversity at opportunity sites and in the protected settlement breaks are  discussed  within  the  Neighbourhood  Plan. There  is  a potential  for  increasing biodiversity through the use of SuDS features such as attenuation basins, ponds and swales in these circumstances.

The area is one of the important open areas in this part of the town that forms part of the overall significance of the Conservation Area. The Conservation Area Character Appraisal identifies that the Cemetery and Rural Museum form a buffer between the housing area of the town and this open land. The verdant and undeveloped nature  of  the  area  contributes  strongly  to  the  character  and  appearance  of  this  part  of  the Conservation Area.

The  land  is  abutted  on  both  sides  by  the Ramsey Rural Museum and the Ramsey 1940s Camp. It  has  historical  significance  through helping  both  of  those  attractions  tell  the story of the history of the town through the various events hosted on the land.

This  space  is  an  integral  part  of  Ramsey’s heritage.  Currently, the field is used for the maximum allowable events throughout the year. It links the Rural Museum and the Ramsey 1940s Camp  and  allows  for  highly  successful  joint  ventures  as  well  as  solo  events.  Without  it,  large community and nationally recognised events will no longer be able to occur causing loss of funding for both the Ramsey 1940s Camp and Ramsey Rural Museum. This could jeopardise the viability of both sites.

Historically, the side of the Museum protruding into the field was identified as an historic track and is adjacent to  what  is  believed  to  be  the  boundary  of  the  Abbey precinct 53 . There is also a possibility of ordinance from the Ramsey 1940s Camp from when it was a searchlight facility during World War II.  The area of the Camp was used during World War I, but documentation associated with  that  appears  to  be  sealed,  possibly  under  the Official Secrets Act.

The area is effectively an events space and showground where  a  significant  number  of  public  events  are  held. These  events  are  integral  to  the  cultural,  social  and  economic  life  of  the  community,  local businesses and attractions. Events held include the 1940s Weekend, the Fen Fair, Country Fair and Plough Day, Ramsey Steam & Fire Show. These events can have up to 3,500 people attending. The  area  of  Ramsey  Town  Moorings  on  the  High  Lode  has  been  partially  altered  through  the development The Moorings off Stocking Fen Road. In around 2022 some 120m of new permanent visitor  moorings  were  completed  on  the eastern  side. The land beyond the bank has recently transferred from the housing developer to Ramsey Town Council.

It  has  historic  significance  as  the  waterway  adjacent  to  the  Corn  Mill  now  known  as  Rivermill Apartments and as part of the nineteenth century industrial area. The  importance  of  the  Ramsey northern gateway goes back to Saxon times, which is the most likely time that the navigable Lodes became the chief form of commercial transport for the town.

The  waterway  has  a  natural  beauty  although  further  enhancement  of  the  public  realm  would improve the overall beauty of this gateway. The eastern side of the moorings has a modern quay; the  western  side  of  the  moorings has an older quayside. The moorings support  recreational  use  of  High Lode  as  a  navigable  waterway  and provides   a   modern   recreational gateway into the town which could be developed further.

82 Theme – Infrastructure
Community Aspirations
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For the Theme – Infrastructure, the following are the community aspirations:
Transport & Parking
The road network across the villages is in a poor  physical condition and a solution to the roads being susceptible and badly impacted by ground movement needs to be explored.

The villages have a lack of footways; in the town the footways are narrow and are a challenge to navigate at certain times, such as on bin day. As the number of bins increases there needs to be exploration into different  solutions, solar  compacting  bins  for  example that  might  assist  in mitigating the size and number of bins on the footway.

Ramsey town has high levels of on-street parking, and the town centre struggles with not having sufficient parking provision to meet the needs of shoppers and those who live and work within the town  centre. Opportunities  to  secure  additional  provision  and  access  to  cost-effective  public electric vehicle charging also need to be explored.
Accessibility/Connectivity

Connectivity between the villages is poor, as is connectivity between the villages and the town. The  geographic  isolation  of  the  parish  means  that  the  provision  of  good  phone  and  internet connection  /  signal/  coverage is  vital. Local  support  for  the services  in  town – dentists, GP’s, district nurses, physios etc. needs to occur. This can include support for these services to diversify their  health  offer  and provide  the  opportunity  for  outreach  hospital services  where  feasible. Hospital facilities are difficult to get to if you do not drive.

Balanced development is wanted to support a thriving community of all ages. Including support for family members to stay in the area throughout their lives; thereby keeping and supporting the local  connection which  is  a  vital  component  of  the  community  spirit  which  was  evident  in  the public consultation responses. Employment opportunities with small start-ups and industrial units as well as shops is important.

Ensuring  that  we  signpost  services  for  those  with  disabilities,  children  and  the  elderly is  an important aspiration. An aging community needs support for aspects like the community bus/ cars to provide connection to the larger towns and cities.

We recognise that the villages around Ramsey are growing and are bringing more traffic, shoppers and people wanting to access services in the town. Due to the poor accessibility and connectivity, new development results in use of the private car rather than active travel modes such as walking and cycling. It is a community aspiration to maintain the culture, the things that make the villages and town unique  and  the  community  feel.  Overall  rural  tourism  is  preferrable  and  more appropriate than housing to maintain that culture.

29.1 The Huntingdonshire   Developer   Contributions SPD 55 sets   out   the   need   to   secure infrastructure and developer contributions from new development in the form of: • Affordable Housing • Green Space • Footpaths and Access • Health • Community Facilities • Libraries and Lifelong Learning • Education and Schools • Residential Wheeled Bins (Note - The costs are updated regularly the 2023/2024 updated costs can be found on the Huntingdonshire website 56 )

29.2 Policy LP  4 - Contributing  to  Infrastructure  Delivery in  the  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to 2036 sets  out  the focus  at  the district level to  secure  infrastructure  and  developer contributions from new development in the form of: • Affordable housing • Recreation (including leisure and sports facilities) • Green infrastructure and biodiversity enhancement/mitigation • Transport • Community facilities • Education, health and social care and community safety • Utilities infrastructure and energy • Emergency and essential services • Environmental improvements • Drainage and flood prevention and protection • Waste recycling facilities • Public art, heritage and archaeology

29.3 The Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) 57 allows local planning authorities to raise funds from  new  development.  The  money  raised  is  used  to  fund  district-wide  and  local infrastructure    projects    that benefit local communities. The CIL charges  are  based  on  the size and type of development. For most developments the CIL charges  are  designed  to  cater for  the required infrastructure provision. For large scale major development 58 there  is  still  a need for infrastructure provision  that  will  not  be  CIL funded.  Therefore section  106 planning  obligations will  still be used as appropriate. The CIL Charging  Schedule 59 has  to  be kept under review with regard to viability considerations so may change during the lifetime of this Neighbourhood Plan.

30. Sustainable Transport

30.1 Local planning policy recognises that Ramsey and the surrounding area has relatively poor transport infrastructure, being well off the primary road network and relatively remote. Its comparatively  limited  services,  facilities  and  employment  opportunities  make  it  a  less sustainable   location   in   terms  of   travel   than   some  of   the  other   market   towns   in Cambridgeshire.

30.2 Ramsey and the surrounding villages are classed as a rural area, there are high levels of car ownership  and  reliance  on  the  car  to  maintain  access  to  key  services. Some  87.7%  of households  in  the  parish  of  Ramsey have  one or  more  cars/vans,  with almost  half  of  the households having two, three or more cars/vans. In addition, high house prices and lack of affordable housing has led to more people travelling further to work, with the average length of commute in Ramsey greater than the national average. Access to employment, education and services can be a real challenge without a car in rural areas.

30.3 The  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to 2036  contains  Policy  LP  16  which indicates that new development will be  expected  to  contribute  to  an enhanced  transport  network  that supports an increasing proportion of journeys    being    undertaken    by sustainable travel modes.

30.4 Access    to    high    quality    public transport  is  known  to  be  hugely beneficial  to  improving  access  to services for  those members of society who cannot,  for a variety of reasons, access a car. This is particularly acute in rural areas such as Ramsey where distances between households and essential services are often large, making walking and cycling less practical than in urban areas. The villages in the parish are reliant upon Ramsey town for many higher order services and facilities. However, the town doesn’t provide all essential services and journeys to larger settlements  such  as  Peterborough or  Huntingdon  are  necessary,  for  example to  access hospital services, higher education and many public services. The Town Council alongside the  Ramsey  Neighbourhood Trust 64 does  look  to  support  the  provision  of  outreach public services to improve accessibility.

30.5 It  has  recently  been  announced  that  there  will  be  a  new  direct  bus  service (X31) from Upwood, Bury and Ramsey to Peterborough from January 2026. This will be operated under the new Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority contract 65 .

30.6 The geographic nature of the parish makes it difficult for residents of the villages to access the services and facilities in Ramsey town centre by walking and cycling. The distances in combination with the lack of footways and uneven road surfaces due to the fenland geology are barriers to walking and cycling.

30.7 The Vision for Ramsey document (extract overleaf) sets out a number of transport initiatives that the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority and Huntingdonshire District Council have developed.

30.8 The  Government  through  Active  Travel  England is  looking  to  make  walking,  wheeling  and cycling the preferred choice for everyone to get around in England. Active travel is the term often  used  to encompass  elements  such  as  walking  to  school,  cycling  to  work,  or  other everyday journeys you make to get from place to place, rather than just walking or cycling solely for leisure or fitness. In addition, active travel can offer a convenient, accessible and affordable way to move more for shorter journeys. National policy in the NPPF does not refer to active travel but instead refers to sustainable transport but includes that policies should look for opportunities to promote walking, cycling and public transport use are identified and  pursued.  Active  travel  and sustainable  travel  modes not  only  positively  contribute  to addressing climate change but also can assist in maintaining a healthy community.

31. Highway Impact

31.1 The  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036  contains Policy  LP  16  on  Sustainable  Travel  and Policy  LP  17 on Parking Provision  and  Vehicle Movement.  This latter policy  indicates  that
Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version)
90 proposals  must incorporate  adequate  parking  for  vehicles  and  cycles.  Advice  on  parking arrangements is contained in the Huntingdonshire Design Guide SPD (2017) 71 .

30.2 Early consultation identified a significant level of concern regarding the volume of traffic and road safety. There was also a significant level of concern about the road infrastructure and  difficulties  with parking.  Improving  road safety  would  enhance  the  quality of life of some of the most vulnerable members of the community. Unfortunately, traffic management is not an issue over which the Town Council has direct control. Most of the traffic originates outside the parish. As a consequence, traffic management cannot be easily addressed by this Neighbourhood  Plan.  However,  the Town  Council will  seek  to  support road  safety improvements around the plan area.

30.3 As part of the overall approach, the Neighbourhood Plan can support and ensure that new development  does  not  adversely  affect  the  highway  network; or  that  where  it  does, contributions through    a    Planning Obligation address     the     impacts appropriately. However, a Planning Obligation can only be sought where it meets the relevant tests; namely: it is necessary  to  make  the  development acceptable   in   planning   terms;   is directly  related  to  the  development; and is fairly and reasonably related in scale   and   kind. In   some cases, Cambridgeshire   County   Council   is seeking  more  direct  off-site  delivery of highway improvements, i.e. rather than paying the County Council a fee the  developer  will  undertake  the  works  in  the highway  directly. As such  in  some  cases  a planning  condition  may  be  the  appropriate  implementation  measure.  In  some cases, Community Infrastructure Levy monies will cover highway improvements.

30.4 The  policy  includes  reference  to the  storage  and  collection  of  refuse  bins as  where insufficient on-site provision is made this can result in a highway impact. This impact involves bins blocking pedestrian use of footways that can lead to pedestrian and vehicle conflict. The Cambridgeshire RECAP Waste Management Design Guide SPD 72 sets out advice on access, maximum travel distances, number of bins per property type etc. and takes into account the Council’s  Waste  Collection  Policies. The  policy looks  to provide  the  opportunity  for developers to promote alternative or innovative methods of storage such as underground bin storage,  for  example on larger sites if viability and operational practicalities support this approach  in  a development. Alternative  or  innovative  methods of storage could have the added benefit of improving the visual aspects of recycling and waste management for the benefit of the community, particularly where smaller dwellings are concentrated, and the provision of wheeled bins may be less desirable.

30.5 Where parking courts are proposed, care needs to be taken. These spaces often suffer from poor  natural surveillance, limited  overlooking  and  can  become  unsafe or underused.  It  is recommended in the policy that parking courts should only be used where they are small, well-overlooked,   incorporate   high   quality   and   subtle   use   of materials,   integrated landscaping and trees. The HDC Design Guide SPD 2017 on page 89 provides more detailed advice.

Policy 9 – Highway Impact

Proposals  will be supported  where they  would  not  adversely  affect  the  local  highway  network. Where proposals would negatively  impact  on  the local highway  network,  contributions  will  be sought, where appropriate, through a Planning Obligation to minimise and mitigate those impacts associated with the development.

Any new development which involves alterations to existing highways and the provision of new highways would be supported where it meets the following design criteria: • Provides suitable measures to accommodate traffic (including at peak times); • Improve the safety and attractiveness of the street scene; and • Integrate appropriate traffic-calming measures within the development.

Development  should  incorporate  adequate dedicated on-site  provision  for  parking within  the curtilage  of  properties  or  in small and  well-overlooked parking  courts  or  similar. Development proposals which would result in the displacement of existing off-street parking provision to on- street parking will not be supported. Proposals that incorporate car-free areas such as play streets would be supported.

New development should incorporate adequate on-site provision for the storage and collection of refuse  bins. Where  appropriate  refuse  collection  storage  should  be  screened  and be easily accessible to the collection point. Where developers want to promote alternative or innovative methods of storage such as underground bin storage where viability and operational practicalities allow this would be supported; particularly where this improves the visual aspects of recycling and waste management for the benefit of the community.
32. Rights of Way Network

32.1 Ramsey covers a large area of countryside and as a consequence it would be expected that it may benefit from an extensive and well-used rights of way network. However, across the parish as a whole there are relatively limited public rights of way. It is possible to get from Ramsey Forty Foot and Ramsey Heights  to Ramsey.  Ramsey St Mary’s by contrast  has  no public rights of way.

32.2 An effective rights of way network provides a dual role for recreation and for sustainable travel. Their recreational use makes an important contribution to health and well-being. The  areas  allocated  for  housing  are  distant  from  the  main services  and  facilities  in Ramsey. As  such  the right of  way network  contributes  to  accessibility  and  providing  the opportunity for sustainable travel using non-vehicle modes. The  Neighbourhood  Plan  looks  to  improve  and  extend  the rights of way network.

32.3 Current provision for pedestrians and cyclists is not significant. Consultation identified the lack of  connection  between  the  villages  and  town  to be  an  issue. There  are  a  number  of footpaths and footways that pass through the town, including footways in the centre of the town that are narrow  and/or  are  in poor quality,  with  the  High  Street being  a  particular example. Narrow streets and on street parking also make cycling difficult and increase the feeling of danger, particularly for young people travelling to school.

Monitoring and Review

34.1 Continual plan review is a fundamental element of the planning system. It is important to check that the plan is being implemented correctly, ensure that outcomes match objectives and to change the plan if they are not.  This Neighbourhood Plan will be carefully monitored by  the Town Council and  reviewed  if  it  becomes  apparent  that  the vision,  goals and objectives of the Plan are not being met.

34.2 Monitoring  is  a  shared  responsibility  of  the Town Council  as  the  qualifying  body; Huntingdonshire  District  Council  as  the  Local  Planning  Authority;  and  users  of  the Neighbourhood Plan. The Town Council will consider the effectiveness of the policies and proposals  in  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  each  time  it  makes  representations  on  a  planning application;  alongside  seeking  views  on  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  at  each  Annual  Parish Meeting. The Town Council will request Huntingdonshire District Council to raise with it any issues  arising  out  of  the  development  management  process  in  determining  individual planning applications. Users of the Neighbourhood Plan are encouraged to make comments on monitoring of the Neighbourhood Plan to the Town Council at any point.

34.3 The Neighbourhood Plan has been prepared to guide development up to 2046. It is unlikely that the Neighbourhood Plan will remain current and entirely relevant for  the entire plan period and may, in whole or in part, require some amendments before 2046.

34.4 There are  a  number  of circumstances  under  which  a  partial  review  of  the  plan  may  be necessary, in accordance with best practice, the Town Council and its partners will consider undertaking a partial review of the Neighbourhood Plan no later than 5 years following its finalisation.

Affordable housing *: Housing for sale or rent, for those whose needs are not met by the market (including housing that provides a subsidised route to home ownership and/or is for essential local workers); and which complies with one or more of the following categories: affordable housing for rent;  starter  homes; discounted  market  sales  housing;  and  other  affordable  routes  to  home ownership including shared ownership, relevant equity loans, other low cost homes for sale (at a price equivalent to at least 20% below local market value) and rent to buy (which includes a period of intermediate rent). Community  Infrastructure  Levy (CIL) *:  A  levy  allowing  local  authorities  to  raise  funds  from owners or developers of land undertaking new building projects in their area.

Neighbourhood plans that have been approved at referendum are also part of the development plan, unless the local planning authority decides that the neighbourhood plan should not be made.
Economic development *: Development, including those within the B and E Use Classes, public and community uses, and main town centre uses (but excluding housing development).

Green  infrastructure: A  network  of  multi-functional  green  and  blue  spaces  and  other  natural features, urban and rural, which is capable of delivering a wide range of environmental, economic, health and wellbeing benefits for nature, climate, local and wider communities and prosperity.

Historic  environment:  All  aspects  of  the  environment  resulting  from  the  interaction  between people and places through time, including all surviving physical remains of past human activity, whether visible, buried or submerged, and landscaped and planted or managed flora.

Planning condition: A condition imposed on a grant of planning permission (in accordance with the Town and Country Planning Act 1990) or a condition included in a Local Development Order or Neighbourhood Development Order.
Planning obligation: A legally enforceable obligation entered into under section 106 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to mitigate the impacts of a development proposal.

Planning  Practice  Guidance  *: this  forms  the  overall  national  planning  practice  guidance  and advice  produced  by  the  Government  to  inform  the  making  of  Development  Plans  including Neighbourhood Plans and decision making on planning applications.
Ramsar  sites:  Wetlands  of  international  importance,  designated  under  the  1971 Ramsar Convention.

Rural exception sites: Small sites used for affordable housing in perpetuity where sites would not normally be used for housing. Rural exception sites seek to address the needs of the local community by accommodating households who are either current residents or have an existing family or employment connection. A proportion of market homes may be allowed on the site at the local planning authority’s discretion, for example where essential to enable the delivery of affordable units without grant funding. [Also see Policy LP 28 of the Local Plan]
Scheduled Monument *: Those monuments that are given legal protection by being scheduled by Historic England.
Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version)

Self-build and custom-build housing:  Housing built by an individual,  a group of individuals, or persons working with or for them, to be occupied by that individual. Such housing can be either market or  affordable housing. A legal definition, for  the purpose of applying the Self-build and Custom Housebuilding Act 2015 (as amended), is contained in section 1(A1) and (A2) of that Act.

Setting of a heritage asset: The surroundings in which a heritage asset is experienced. Its extent is not fixed and may change as the asset and its surroundings evolve. Elements of a setting may make a positive or negative contribution to the significance of an asset, may affect the ability to appreciate that significance or may be neutral.

Settlement  Boundary *: The  boundary  drawn  around  various  towns  and  villages  to  limit  new development and define the ‘built-up area’ of the settlement. Outside of the settlement boundary is considered to be the countryside.

Significance (for heritage policy): The value of a heritage asset to this and future generations because  of  its  heritage  interest.  The  interest  may  be  archaeological,  architectural,  artistic  or historic. Significance derives not only from a heritage asset’s physical presence, but also from its setting.  For  World  Heritage  Sites,  the  cultural value described within each site’s Statement of Outstanding Universal Value forms part of its significance.

Special  Areas  of  Conservation  (SAC):  Areas  defined  by  regulation  3  of  the  Conservation  of Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  which  have  been  given  special  protection  as  important conservation sites.

Special  Protection  Areas  (SPA):  Areas  classified  under  regulation  15  of  the  Conservation  of Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  which  have  been  identified  as  being  of  international importance for the breeding, feeding, wintering or the migration of rare and vulnerable species of birds.
Site  of  Special Scientific  Interest:  Sites designated  by  Natural  England  under  the  Wildlife  and Countryside Act 1981.

Strategic Environmental Assessment: A procedure (set out in the Environmental Assessment of Plans and Programmes Regulations 2004) which requires the formal environmental assessment of certain plans and programmes which are likely to have significant effects on the environment.

Supplementary planning documents: Documents which add further detail to the policies in the Local Plan. They can be used to provide further guidance for development on specific sites, or on particular  issues,  such  as  design.  Supplementary  planning  documents  are  capable  of  being  a material consideration in planning decisions but are not part of the development plan.

Sustainable transport modes: Any efficient, safe and accessible means of transport with overall low  impact  on  the  environment,  including  walking  and  cycling,  low  and  ultra-low  emission vehicles, car sharing and public transport.
Windfall sites: Sites not specifically identified in the development plan.

metadata.title: Huntingdonshire teenager becomes country's youngest bookmaker at 18
metadata.contentSnippet: A Huntingdonshire teenager has swapped plumbing training to become the country's youngest bookmaker.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdonshire teenager becomes country's youngest bookmaker at 18
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire teenager has swapped plumbing training to become the country's youngest bookmaker. Archie Bailey, 18, from Hartford has joined his proud dad Steve in working as an on-course bookmaker at racecourses across the country. He joined Steve within days of turning 18 earlier this summer. Steve lives in Peterborough and previously ran an estate agency in March. Archie Bailey loves working alongside his dad Steve on racecourses across the country. (Image: Marilyn Bailey) The father and son trade under the name of Stevie Stretch. Archie's mum, Marilyn also from Hartford, said her son had been doing a plumbing apprenticeship, but decided it was not for him, and instead decided to join his dad in the paddock. The teenager has always had an interest in betting and felt the move into the industry was the natural step to take so he could help grow the family business while testing his own skills of the betting market. Archie Bailey has become the country's youngest bookie. (Image: Marilyn Bailey) Archie has already shown he can read the betting markets and hopes to gain experience alongside other bookmakers before taking the family business forward. Bookmaking has also become something of a family tradition, with Steve’s 91-year-old father previously accompanying him to racecourses and working alongside him on pitches. Marilyn said Steve is delighted to have their son working alongside him now his own father is unable to attend meetings. Archie Bailey loves working alongside his dad Steve on racecourses across the country. (Image: Marilyn Bailey) Alongside his work with his father, Archie works as an introducing broker for a day trading company specialising in gold. Marilyn said he is also keen to broaden his experience by working for other bookmakers.

metadata.title: Undercover female officers run county's streets in crackdown on harassment
metadata.contentSnippet: Police are targeting parts of Cambridgeshire after more than three-quarters of women in a survey said they had felt unsafe while running.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Undercover female officers run county's streets in crackdown on harassment
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police are targeting parts of Cambridgeshire after more than three-quarters of women in a survey said they had felt unsafe while running. Cambridgeshire Constabulary’s Operation Vexa is focused on preventing harassment and other offending in public spaces, with activity being directed towards locations where women reported experiencing problems. The first undercover operation was held in Huntingdon on Monday night when a group of female officers ran a circuit around the town, including Hinchingbrooke Park, which was one of the areas highlighted in the survey. Det Supt Dave Taylor gives his team a briefing before the first night of action in Huntingdon as part of Operation Vexa aimed at improving women's safety. (Image: Sarah Cliss) They were backed up by male officers in uniform in vehicles ready to act if the need arose during the hour-long exercise. The women completed their run without incident, but runner Det Supt Denise Harper said many women do not enjoy the same freedom. "When I was asked about this operation, I volunteered to do it straight away. I feel very passionately about keeping women and girls safe," she said. "It's not right that women and girls have to put certain measures in place, and think about their personal safety when they are trying to go about normal activities like exercising and running." Before the women took to their heels on the 3.2 mile circuitous run, they and their male colleagues were given a pre-operation briefing by Det Supt Dave Taylor, who is the leading officer responsible for protecting vulnerable people for Cambridgeshire. He explained to the team, alongside representatives from the media, the importance of Operation Vexa, which this week will see two further exercises in Cambridge and Peterborough. He said the operation aimed to prevent and tackle offending by identifying perpetrators before their behaviour escalates. Two of the female officers who ran the streets of Huntingdon in the first of three nights of action as part of Operation Vexa. (Image: Sarah Cliss) He said 2,149 women had responded to a public survey conducted in August with more than three-quarters saying they felt unsafe while running. Only three per cent had reported their concerns to police, he said. Det Supt Taylor said: "That means just because it is not being reported, it is not happening. I am hoping this operation will increase women's confidence reporting offences to the police." More than half, 54 per cent of those who took part in the survey, said they had experienced harassment and 64 per cent said they had been cat-called. Det Supt Denise Harper was among the women runners. She said she felt passionately about trying to improve the safety of women and girls on Cambridgeshire's streets. (Image: Sarah Cliss) The team will carry out a similar operation along Cambridge’s riverside corridor on Wednesday before moving to Peterborough on Friday. Det Supt Taylor said early evening and the hours after dark were key deployment times. But he warned that harassment can happen in daylight and that a lack of recorded incidents does not mean there is no risk. Det Supt Taylor said women’s experiences had shaped the operation. He said: “We are listening to runners’ experiences and using them for targeted prevention activity. “These operations are being carried out in areas where women who responded to the survey told us they have experienced problems. “Through this operation we want to target poor behaviour and criminal offences to enable women to be and feel safer in public spaces.” He described Operation Vexa as a “perpetrator-focused prevention and enforcement activity in public spaces”. The operation aims to prevent harm, deter harassment, identify repeat or escalating behaviour and intervene when offences or risks require police action. Officers will also use the deployments to build intelligence about concerning behaviour, people, vehicles, locations and times, while Det Supt Taylor emphasised the force takes women's safety seriously, and wants to increase their confidence that reports of harassment and sexualised behaviour will be taken seriously. The briefing listed possible incidents, including sexualised comments, gestures or approaches, being followed on foot, by bicycle, e-scooter or vehicle, stalking, assault and threatened violence. The plain-clothes officers were to report concerning behaviour, locations and risks while following agreed routes and staying in contact with colleagues throughout the run. Uniformed male officers were there to intervene if needed to safeguard people, make an arrest or preserve evidence. The force said its aim is to make Cambridgeshire’s public spaces safer by preventing harm where women have reported harassment or fear. Det Supt Taylor said women should not have to change where, when or how they exercise because they fear harassment. The operation also draws on the Angiolini Inquiry, which found that women routinely change their routes, plans and behaviour because of safety fears. The briefing said offences and concerning behaviour in public spaces can go unreported and unrecorded. It says non-contact and early-stage sexual behaviour should be taken seriously because it may be part of a pattern that repeats or escalates. Operation Vexa is part of the constabulary’s wider response to violence against women and girls. It aims to prevent offending and change perpetrators’ behaviour instead of asking women to change their routines.

metadata.title: DWP Winter Fuel Payment warning as pensioners say they have to wrap up in blankets
metadata.contentSnippet: Many fear they will be forced to sit in freezing homes and wrap themselves in blankets this winter as household energy bills are set to jump by 26% in January.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP Winter Fuel Payment warning as pensioners say they have to wrap up in blankets
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Pensioners fear they will be forced to sit in freezing homes and wrap themselves in blankets this winter as household energy bills are set to jump by 26% in January. Charities have warned the price rise could leave older people struggling to afford to heat their homes - despite DWP winter fuel payments - while terminally ill people face the added worry of keeping vital medical equipment running and maintaining a warm environment. Age UK and palliative care charity Sue Ryder have both called for targeted energy support for those most at risk as the cost of keeping warm rises. One in five pensioner households in Great Britain are likely to be in “fuel stress” this winter, Age UK explained of its analysis. This means they will spend more than 10% of their after-tax household income on energy bills. Among the poorest households – those in the bottom 20% of the income distribution – almost half are expected to be in this position. The charity estimates the average pensioner household will spend £1 in every £14 of its income on gas and electricity at the forecast prices. Caroline Abrahams, charity director at Age UK, said the latest increase “will be deeply worrying for many older people who are already anxious about how they will afford to keep warm this winter”. While welcoming the Government's £100 energy payment for households from January, and winter fuel payments more broadly, she warned it was “simply not enough”. She added: “Another increase in energy bills risks pushing more households into hardship at a time when keeping warm is not a luxury, but an essential part of protecting their health. “Our recent analysis suggests that this winter is set to be extremely challenging for pensioners who are struggling to afford the energy they need. That’s why we believe ministers should introduce an emergency energy support package targeted at those households most at risk of cold homes, financial hardship and worsening health this winter.” Three pensioners in their 80s have spoken about the difficult choices they fear they will face as bills rise. Roger, who did not give his surname, described the 26% increase as “unbelievable” and said it “will lead to utter despair” for many older people. He works in a care home and said he can still “balance the books”, but added: “It worries me what might happen if I’m unable to work one day”. Sheila, who also did not give her surname, said she had not used her central heating for years and instead relied on a couple of electric heaters in whichever room she was in. She said that on particularly cold nights she was “often left sitting in a cold house, wrapping myself up in blankets”. Age UK is encouraging older people on low incomes who are struggling with their bills to contact its free advice line on 0800 169 65 65 or visit www.ageuk.org.uk/money . The rise in energy costs could also have serious consequences for people living with terminal illnesses, Sue Ryder warned. Dr Paul Perkins, the charity's chief medical director, said the increase could “darken the precious time they have left”. Recommended reading: He said: “It may make them anxious and afraid, wondering how they’re going to keep themselves warm and keep their medical equipment going when they should be spending time making memories with loved ones. “Many rely on higher levels of heating to stop symptoms worsening, while others depend on vital electrical medical equipment, which in some cases is keeping them alive. All this leaves them with significantly increased costs. “Targeted help with energy costs would remove a substantial burden and allow people to make the most of the time they have left, not spending it watching their bank balance. Everyone deserves to live well and with dignity until the very end.” Tomorrow morning, Ofgem will announce the Jan-March energy price cap. It's likely to go up 26% but what after that? And does this mean you should fix? A clip from my Martin Lewis Money Show energy special tonight. Watch the full thing for far more help: https://t.co/Vcrj5Jywiw https://t.co/yR2mlzgyBw — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 24, 2026 Becca Stacey, from end-of-life care charity Marie Curie, said: “No energy support scheme specifically targets people living with terminal illness, despite extensive evidence of higher bills and significant financial hardship at the end of life.” She said support available through the £100 household energy payment, £150 Warm Home Discount and £300 Winter Fuel Payment “covers just a quarter of an average household’s energy bills”. Marie Curie is calling for a 50% energy social tariff for people living with a terminal illness. The charity said its modelling suggests this could lift up to 54,000 people – 45% of those dying – out of fuel poverty. Have you turned your heating on yet? Tell us in the comments below...

metadata.title: 10 commonly misunderstood UK road signs - how many can you recognise?
metadata.contentSnippet: Understand ten road signs, including no vehicles, toad crossings, clearways and pass either side.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 commonly misunderstood UK road signs - how many can you recognise?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A blank red-ringed road sign bans vehicles, including bicycles unless they are being pushed. It is one of several signs whose meaning might not be immediately obvious to drivers. The Department for Transport groups traffic signs into three basic types: those that give orders, warn road users or provide information. Here are ten signs and what they mean, using guidance from the Highway Code and sign maker Hirst Signs. This board tells drivers that another sign is not currently in use, according to Hirst Signs. The company says it may cover a temporary speed limit, a roadworks warning or a diversion that is no longer in place. A sign showing a vehicle and an explosion means vehicles carrying explosives are prohibited. It is a restriction on what the vehicle is carrying, rather than a warning that other cars might explode. This triangular warning sign means slow-moving military vehicles are likely to be in or crossing the road ahead. Hirst Signs says the sign may appear near military bases. A red-bordered sign showing a horse-drawn vehicle means those vehicles are prohibited. It is different from a warning sign telling drivers that horse-drawn vehicles may be on the road. A warning sign with a lightning-shaped symbol alerts road users to an overhead electric cable. The Highway Code says an accompanying plate indicates the maximum height of vehicles that can pass safely. A white circle with a red border means no vehicles, rather than just no motor vehicles. The Highway Code says bicycles can pass if they are being pushed, but not ridden. Check any accompanying plate, which may give times or other qualifications to a restriction. A triangular sign featuring a toad warns drivers of a migratory toad crossing ahead. Hirst Signs says the warning is used where toads cross the road, particularly during breeding season. A triangular sign bearing the word “Ford” warns that the road crosses a stream or river. Water levels can rise in poor weather, so a crossing that is normally shallow may become hazardous. A blue circle with a red border and red cross means no stopping on a clearway. The restriction applies to the main carriageway at any time. A blue circular sign with two white arrows means vehicles may pass on either side to reach the same destination. Unlike a keep-left sign, it allows a choice of which side to use.

metadata.title: Plans for nurse-led care home in Hunts village
metadata.contentSnippet: Plans submitted to turn Little Orchard in Catworth, Huntingdonshire, into a nurse-led care home for six residents, with 24-hour staff and a day centre.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Plans for nurse-led care home in Hunts village
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans have been submitted to expand a community hub in a Huntingdonshire village into a nurse-led care home. A retrospective application to Huntingdonshire District Council (HDC) seeks to change the use of the property at 41 Station Road in Catworth from a home to a small residential care home and day centre, known as Little Orchard. The care home would provide permanent accommodation for six residents, each with their own room, and communal areas, with nursing staff on duty 24 hours a day. The previous use of the property was a 7-bedroom dwelling with associated parking and garage (class C3), but the plans would see the use change to class C2. The planning statement submitted with the application, from operator Golden Community, said the facility would offer companionship, activities, nutritional support, and nurse-led wellbeing oversight. Golden Community already operates Little Orchard Community Hub which offers day activities, hobbies, social groups, meals, refreshments, health drop-in sessions and support for adults, but hopes to expand into a small care home. On their website, the organisation states: "Our vision is to provide an alternative to a traditional large care-home environment: a small, familiar and homely setting with nursing support, beautiful communal spaces, private rooms and access to the wider Little Orchard community." The plans state that residents would not have private vehicles, and visitor appointments would be staggered to manage traffic. All parking associated with the development would be accommodated within the site, which has nine parking spaces, including four staff spaces, three visitor spaces, one accessible space, and a dedicated ambulance bay. No additional parking spaces are proposed. At least two members of staff would be on duty at all times when the nursing home is operating, with staffing levels increasing if residents' needs become greater. Full details on the planning application are available on the HDC planning portal using reference 26/02108/FUL.

metadata.title: 10 pubs in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once
metadata.contentSnippet: Looking for the best place to buy a pint or book a Sunday roast, but don't know where to look? Don't worry, we've got you covered.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 pubs in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Looking for the best place to buy a pint or book a Sunday roast, but don't know where to look? Don't worry, we've got you covered. Let's be honest, when it comes to finding a proper local, we're truly spoilt for choice in Cambridgeshire. So, to help you make up your mind, we've rounded up 10 incredible pubs you have to visit at least once. A multi‑award‑winning riverside pub near the River Great Ouse, known for refined, seasonal cooking and a serious wine list. Regularly recommended in dining guides, it balances white‑tablecloth quality with a relaxed country‑pub atmosphere and a pretty garden that comes into its own in summer. It boasts a rating of 4.3 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 1,250 reviews and 4.5 stars out of 5 on Google. A handsome thatched pub near the Northamptonshire border, The Pheasant majors on polished modern British dishes and an impressive drinks list. Inside you’ll find beams, open fires and an intimate dining room, making it a strong choice for special‑occasion suppers and long Sunday lunches. It boasts a rating of 4.4 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 800 reviews and 4.7 stars out of 5 on Google. Grade II‑listed and set in a picture‑postcard village, The Crown Inn blends flagstone and beams character with creative, seasonal menus. Reviewers highlight its warm welcome, generous roasts and restaurant‑quality food, while the bar still feels like a proper village hub. It boasts a rating of 4.6 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 881 reviews and 4.7 stars out of 5 on Google. Right on the riverside, The Cutter pairs big views of the river with crowd‑pleasing pub favourites and a busy terrace. It’s popular with boaters, walkers and day‑trippers, who rate the relaxed atmosphere, hearty portions and the chance to watch the world go by with a pint. It boasts a rating of 4.3 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 1,250 reviews and 4.5 stars out of 5 on Google. A well‑regarded micropub in Ely’s centre, the Drayman’s Son specialises in cask and craft beer in a compact, sociable space. Expect rotating local brews, knowledgeable staff and a friendly chat-over-pints vibe rather than loud music or big‑screen sport. It boasts a rating of 4.8 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 183 reviews and 4.8 stars out of 5 on Google. Near the riverside, The Acre is praised for its home‑cooked Sunday carvery, friendly service and relaxed, dog‑friendly feel. A pleasant outdoor area makes it a good summer stop‑off, especially for narrowboaters and walkers exploring Fenland waterways. It boasts a rating of 4.4 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off 319 reviews. Overlooking the River Great Ouse, near Littleport, this inn offers riverside drinking, dining and rooms. Visitors highlight welcoming staff, solid pub classics and the appeal of sitting by the water with a drink after a walk or cycle along the river. It boasts a rating of 3.7 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off 74 reviews and 4.3 stars out of 5 on Google. Set by a village green near Oundle, The Chequered Skipper draws strong reviews for its charming setting and quality food. Inside feels country‑cosy, while the green‑side tables are ideal for summer evenings and family gatherings. It boasts a rating of 4.8 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 90 reviews and 4.5 stars out of 5 on Google. A quirky Peterborough fixture, Charters is a real‑ale bar on a converted Dutch barge moored on the Nene. Known for its beer range, live music and relaxed atmosphere, it’s a distinctive spot for riverside drinks close to the city centre. It boasts a rating of 4.1 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 130 reviews and 4.6 stars out of 5 on Google. Tucked in North Street, the historic Ostrich Inn is one of the city’s most characterful pubs. It combines real ale and simple pub dishes with regular live music and events, earning a loyal following among locals and visitors seeking atmosphere over slickness. It boasts a rating of 3.9 out of 5 on Tripadvisor based off more than 40 reviews and 4.6 stars out of 5 on Google. Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: CQC recognises significant improvements across East of England Ambulance Service
metadata.contentSnippet: An ambulance service has been rated “Good” after inspectors found major improvements in staffing and patient access.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: CQC recognises significant improvements across East of England Ambulance Service
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An ambulance service has been rated “good” after inspectors found major improvements in staffing and patient access. The East of England Ambulance Service NHS Trust (EEAST) welcomed the Care Quality Commission’s (CQC) latest findings on its Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) and Urgent and Emergency Care (UEC) services. Inspectors rated the trust’s EOC “Good” overall and in all five areas assessed: safe, effective, caring, responsive and well-led. Urgent and Emergency Care was also rated “Good” in all five areas, with the CQC praising improvements in safety, responsiveness and leadership. The findings represent a turnaround from the regulator's previous inspection in November 2024, when concerns were raised about staffing levels and how quickly patients could access services. Following that inspection, the CQC served a Section 29A Warning Notice after finding the trust in breach of regulations relating to staffing and safe care and treatment. Inspectors said the service lacked enough staff with the right skills, qualifications and experience, while call waiting times fell below national standards. During the latest inspection, however, the regulator found improvements had been made to call handling and dispatch times and that the EOC was no longer in breach of those regulations. The CQC also found faster ambulance responses in Urgent and Emergency Care and said the service had met the warning notice’s requirements. Inspectors praised progress in staffing, mandatory training, appraisals, safeguarding, call handling, dispatch and ambulance response times. The CQC inspected the trust’s three Emergency Operations Centres in Bedford, Norwich and Chelmsford and spoke to call handlers, dispatchers, clinical co-ordinators and managers. Inspectors also examined six ambulance bases and held seven focus groups as part of their assessment of Urgent and Emergency Care, speaking to around 105 members of staff. They also accompanied ambulance crews responding to urgent calls and reviewed policies and procedures. EEAST provides emergency ambulance services 24 hours a day across Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire, Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, covering around 7,500 square miles and a population of more than 6.2 million people. The CQC did not speak directly to patients because its Emergency Operations Centre inspection had no patient-facing element. Inspectors praised improvements in workforce capacity and performance, including the trust’s Cardiac Arrest Desk initiative. Neill Moloney, chief executive of EEAST, said: "These findings recognise the enormous amount of work colleagues across EEAST have put into improving our services for patients. "The progress reflected in these reports is a testament to their professionalism, commitment and determination to deliver high-quality care every day. "We are proud that the CQC has recognised these improvements." Mr Moloney admitted more work was needed, particularly to make leadership and management consistently effective across Urgent and Emergency Care. He added: "We also recognise the areas of continued focus identified by the CQC, particularly around ensuring leadership and management arrangements are consistently effective across all parts of our Urgent and Emergency Care service, and we remain committed to building on the progress we have made." The earlier Section 29A notice also covered failures in investigating and mitigating controlled-drug incidents, service culture and using staff feedback to improve services.

Horror at Hinchingbrooke House, once a local seasonal attraction, grew to become one of the UK's most recognised Halloween events. It attracted people from all across the country flocking to the grounds of the Huntingdon school for a scare. Skylark boasts boasts a rating of 4.4 out of 5 on Tripadvisor, with more than 290 'excellent' reviews. Meanwhile, its rated 4.4 out of 5 based off more than 1,600 visitor reviews on Google. Visitors frequently praise the garden centre's "friendly staff", "well-organised activities", and "value for money". One visitor said: "The activities have been thought out really well and there is just enough time on each activity to hold a child's interest but not to get bored." Another added: "This is the most amazing day out. Complete value for money. Get there when it opens and stay all day. You'll need that to get round all the attractions." A third guest said: "There was a lot to enjoy and all very well spaced out. It never felt crowded. Plenty of food options. There were lots of staff members on hand to help the children." metadata.title: Aldi trialling changes to some of its UK stores that shoppers might notice
metadata.contentSnippet: Aldi has confirmed it will be trialling changes to some of its UK stores by reducing the number of products it sells.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Aldi trialling changes to some of its UK stores that shoppers might notice
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The budget supermarket Aldi has confirmed it will be making some changes to a range of its UK stores. Aldi hopes the changes will help the store remain efficient and keep prices low compared to other supermarkets. The brand will be trialling reducing the number of products it sells in some of its stores across the UK. The changes come after being “outpaced” by Lidl in its sales growth over the last three years, according to The Grocer. Over the past year, Lidl’s market share has grown from 8.2% to 8.6% with its sales rising by 6.6% year on year. For Aldi, sales have grown by 0.4% year on year with the supermarket’s share dropping from 10.5% to 10.4%. An Aldi spokesperson said: “As a discounter, we’ve always kept things simple so that we can deliver what matters most to our customers – award-winning quality at everyday low prices.” The brand will be making similar changes to its stores in Europe including Switzerland and Germany. Aldi regularly reviews what items it produces and the range of products available in its stores to reflect what customers want. A report from the Competition & Markets Authority (CMA) that was released in August said Aldi’s core grocery range features around 4,000 to 5,000 products when counting different flavours and temporary lines. More than 90% of the products are from Aldi’s own brand. The report said Aldi had understated the size of its grocery range by around 40% with the brand saying it had around 2,000 to 3,000 products. Lidl had similar differences in the number of products it claimed it sold compared to what the report found. Recommended reading Lidl sells a few hundred more products compared to Aldi with around 80% to 90% being from its own label. Aldi’s spokesperson added: “Our volume sales are growing ahead of the market, and we’ve welcomed an additional 140,000 shoppers through our doors in the past 12 weeks as customers recognise that the simple everyday low prices we offer can help them get more value from their weekly shop.” Do you prefer to shop at Aldi or Lidl? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis says £100 energy payment 'won't cover' January bill increase
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Lewis has warned households to prepare for a huge jump in energy bills after Ofgem confirmed today (November 25) that the price cap will rise by 26% in January. The Money Saving Expert founder discussed the looming increase on his television show last night, warning that households could face an extra £160 to £170 in energy costs over just three months. His forecast proved remarkably close to the figure confirmed by regulator Ofgem this morning, with the new price cap set at £2,166 a year for a typical household using gas and electricity and paying by Direct Debit. This is an increase of £443 compared with the current annualised figure of £1,723, and will affect around 20 million households on variable tariffs. The confirmed increase means the price cap will reach its highest level in almost four years , putting further pressure on households already struggling with the cost of living. Martin also warned that the headline 26% increase would not affect every household in the same way, with gas users potentially facing a much bigger jump than electricity-only households. He explained that the increase was being driven primarily by the amount people pay for each unit of energy, rather than standing charges. Speaking on his show, he said: "But this is the really big thing to look at: standing charges not up that much. The unit rates, the amount you pay for each unit of gas and electricity, that is where the big rise is going to come from. "Electricity up 24%, gas up 37%." Tomorrow morning, Ofgem will announce the Jan-March energy price cap. It's likely to go up 26% but what after that? And does this mean you should fix? A clip from my Martin Lewis Money Show energy special tonight. Watch the full thing for far more help: https://t.co/Vcrj5Jywiw https://t.co/yR2mlzgyBw — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 24, 2026 The warning also comes after Chancellor John Healey announced a one-off £100 Household Energy Payment for around 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. The money is expected to start reaching eligible households in January 2027, but Martin warned it would not be enough to offset the increase in energy costs for most people. He said: "That is a rise of £160 to £170 just from January to the end of March, not 2027. Just January to the end of March. "The government energy support of £100 is paid in January for those in council tax bands A to D, it will not cover the rise for most households." The Government's £100 payment will therefore provide some help, but households could still face a significant shortfall. Martin also used last night's programme to examine whether households should consider moving away from their current variable energy tariff and locking into a fixed deal - but explained that every situation is different. He warned that energy prices could remain substantially higher throughout 2027, although he stressed that forecasts further into the year were much less certain. He said: "If those predictions are right, and this is pretty certain, it is going to be substantially higher throughout 2027 than it is now." Martin then highlighted the cheapest two-year fixed deal available at the time of his programme, which was around 2% more expensive than the existing price cap. That means customers choosing the deal would initially pay slightly more over the remaining weeks of the current price cap period. However, if the January forecasts proved correct, he said they could save more than 20% between January and March, with potentially further savings over the following year - but while it is good to consider options, circumstances will vary. Recommended reading : He was careful not to guarantee that switching would save money, saying: "I cannot tell you that fixing will save you money because I would need a crystal ball, but I can tell you the vast balance of probabilities means it will save you money over the next year." He added: "And if you are risk averse and want to avoid those January price hikes, fixing is the sensible option if you are on the price cap." As always, households should compare available tariffs against their own energy usage and check any exit fees before switching, as the cheapest deal will vary depending on where they live and how much energy they use.

held at 7pm on Thursday 27 August 2026 at  
Ramsey Town Council Great Whyte, Ramsey 
 
 
Present:  Councillors: I Axelsen, J Bufton, J Clarke, M Clarke, V Fendley (Mayor), S Fice, R 
Terrill, J Thompson, and  L Webster. 
In attendance: Mrs A Jerrom, Deputy Town Clerk  
 
The Chairman welcomed new Councillor Jessie Thompson to the meeting. 
 
289. Apologies for Absence. 
Cllrs J Aubin, A Austin, S Corney, A Costello, L Knight, C Maskell and P Rose. 
 
290.To Receive Declarations of Interest. 
No declarations of interest were made. 
 
291. Public Participation. 
There were no members of the public present. 
 
292. Minutes of the Last Meeting to be Approved. 
Councillors  voted with  two  abstentions to  accept  the Minutes  of the meeting  of the  Council 
held on 13
th
 August 2026 as a correct record. 
 
293. Planning Applications for Consideration. 
1.1 26/01416/HHFUL – Two  storey extension,  barn and  carport,  internal  and  external 
alterations,  new  dormer and  canopy  roofs  and  installation  of  solar  PV  panels – Heathfield, 
Benwick Road, Ramsey Forty Foot  Proposed by Cllr S Fice and seconded by Cllr L Webster 
Ramsey Town Council voted unanimously for Huntingdonshire District Council to APPROVE 
the application as per their decision on a previous application for the property in June 2026, 
which had since been withdrawn. 
1.2  26/01206/OUT – Proposed  demolition  of  an  existing  dwelling  and  outbuilding  and 
replacement  with  4  new  dwellings  (outline  application with  all  matters  reserved,  with  the 
exception of access) – 190 Herne Road, Ramsey St Marys.  Having been proposed by Cllr J 
Clarke and seconded by Cllr Terrill, councillors voted unanimously to recommend refusal of the 
application  due  to  the  lack  of information  regarding adequate parking,  particularly  for  the 
bungalows  at  the  rear  of  the  development.    They  also had  concerns  regarding  the  possible 
precedent that might be set for development at the rear of properties in the village. 
1.3 26/01484/TREE – G1  (dead  Silver  Birch) – fell  and remove – Cedar  Lodge,  St Marys 
Road,  Ramsey. Having  been  proposed  by  Cllr  S  Fice  and  seconded  by  Cllr  L  Webster 
councillors voted unanimously to make no observations either in favour or against the proposal 
but to leave the decision to the arboricultural officer. 
 
294.  Consultation on the Reviewed Bury Draft Neighbourhood Plan. 
Councillors discussed the suggested response to the consultation previously circulated by 
Cllr Fendley. It was agreed that there would be infrastructure implications for Ramsey 
following the growth within the Bury Neighbourhood Plan area. It was therefore proposed by 
Cllr Bufton, seconded by Cllr Terrill and agreed with one abstention to submit that response 
from the Town Council which included the acknowledgment of the need for Infrastructure 
Levy(CIL) contributions towards car parking provision at Mews Close and electric charging 
points which would serve the wider community. 
 
 
 

2 
 
295. Update on Emergency Response – Holme Fen. 
Councillor Fendley provided an update on the huge operation to support the Fire Service 
while they were attending the recent fires at Holme Fen.  In answer to a request for 
emergency assistance from HDC the Mayor and Town Clerk had organised for food supplies 
to be provided to the firemen alongside that already organised by the Admiral Wells in Holme 
and Cllr Fendley had set up a Go Fund Me page for donations. There had been an amazing 
response from the community, with volunteers and local businesses providing food over the 
weekend and following days.  Cllr Fendley reported that the firemen had been overwhelmed 
by the response and hard work of all concerned and they would be issuing formal letters of 
thanks. There would be a further update on the Go Fund Me funds at the next meeting of the 
Town Council.  The Chief Fire Officer had been invited to attend the Mayor’s Civic Service in 
September. 
 
296. Meeting Dates 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council would take place on Thursday 10th September 
at 7pm.

held at 7pm on Thursday 13 August 2026 at  
Ramsey Town Council Great Whyte, Ramsey

Fendley (Mayor), L Knight, C Maskell, R Terrill, L Webster, and E Welsh. 
In attendance: Mrs L Renfree, Town Clerk

There were 10 members of the public present.
