metadata.title: St Ives wine bar allowed to open later after ‘error’ in earlier application
metadata.contentSnippet: St Ives wine bar Broadway Cellars can open later after a planning error, with Huntingdonshire District Council approving extended Sunday and weekday hours.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Ives wine bar allowed to open later after ‘error’ in earlier application
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A wine bar has been given permission to open later on Sundays and weekdays after an “error” was made on an earlier application. Broadway Cellars opened in St Ives late last year and has since become a popular destination in the historic market town. The bar applied to Huntingdonshire District Council to extend its opening hours until midnight on Thursdays and 1am on Fridays and Saturdays, which was approved. The business at 34 The Broadway previously had to close at 11pm from Wednesday to Saturday and also applied to host live music on Fridays and Saturdays. But a further application was made after an error in the application meant the bar was still limited to closing at 7pm on Mondays, Tuesdays and Sundays. The bar had sought to extend this until 11pm on Mondays and Tuesdays and midnight on Wednesdays and Sundays. A report from HDC’s planning officers said they “understand there was an error with the earlier submission” and “so a further amendment to the opening hours is being sought under this application”. Despite having a licence to open later, a condition on the planning application meant the bar was unable to do so. St Ives Town Council supported the extension they said “would be consistent” with “other pubs in the area” and “acknowledged the success of Broadway Cellars”. The combined bar and wine shop offers not just a wide range of wine to purchase but also cocktails and beers. As a condition of their licence a CCTV system has to be installed and maintained with recordings kept for 31 consecutive days.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A family friendly venue with coffee shop, restaurant and bar all rolled into one has been hailed the "coolest place" by visitors. The Yard is tucked away on Newnham Street, in Ely, and was described as the city's "latest treat" when it opened. Silver Oak Coffee, Ely's independent coffee roastery owned by Susanne Stent and Bruce Garside, opened the venue in March 2023. It is described as a "proper independent venue" (Image: The Yard) More than 600 guests poured into the "gorgeous" new venue when it opened, which is spread over five shipping containers. It features a children’s play area, coffee shop, restaurant, bar and outdoor seating area and was designed as a space that "brings people together". On its website, The Yard proudly describes itself as a "proper independent venue run by people who care about every detail, from the playlist to the pour". Naturally, The Yard has received dozens of raving reviews on Trip Advisor, with more than 50 rating the venue as "excellent" One visitor said: "The Yard feels like one of those places that instantly lifts the mood — informal, creative, and full of life." The Yard serves "seasonal, locally-sourced food that goes way beyond standard pub grub" and boasts a bar team of "cocktail nerds" and "whiskey geeks". The Yard opened its doors in March 2023 (Image: The Yard) "Community is at the heart of everything we do. We support local artists, musicians, and suppliers. "We host art exhibitions, give platforms to emerging talent, and try to make sure that every person who walks through our doors feels like they belong." Have you got a story you want to share? The venue opened its doors "to a great hoorah" in November 2024 and owner Juliana Hunt believes the meat on offer is the best in the county. The restaurant first opened in November 2024 (Image: Griddle Bar and Meat House) On its website, the restaurant proudly describes itself as being "dedicated to serving the finest quality steaks and handcrafted beers". As well as the "finest selection of premium meats", a range of "tastebud-challenging" beers are on offer, including the Slippery Elly and Sniggler's Hat. Griddle Bar and Meat House has racked up raving reviews, with visitors praising it "great food" and "beautiful" craft beer. One visitor said: "I recently tried the craft beer at Griddle Bar and Meat House. It poured a beautiful, hazy golden with a white head. Just last year, its burgers were ranked among the best in Cambridgeshire by Cambridge Foodies. "If you haven't tried our burgers, we have got everything you need to satisfy those cravings," a spokesperson said. "From juicy classics to mouthwatering specials, come and taste why we're one of the best." Have you got a story you want to share? Described as a "lovely gem", nature lovers can't help but rave about Paxton Pits Nature Reserve. A tranquil wildlife haven nestled in Little Paxton, the reserve has earned glowing praise from visitors for its peaceful atmosphere, scenic beauty and diverse wildlife. On TripAdvisor, the reserve has more than 150 'excellent' reviews, with visitors recommending it as a must visit for families and nature lovers. Elsewhere, on Google Reviews, Paxton Pits has a score of 4.7 out of 5 from more than 99 reviews. Covering 77 hectares, the reserve features a variety of habitats, including lakes, meadow, grassland, scrub, and woodland. It is managed by Huntingdonshire District Council in partnership with the Friends of Paxton Pits. Just last year, Paxton Pits Nature Reserve was a recipient of the coveted Green Flag Award. Recognising the best parks and green spaces internationally, the scheme provides the high standards against which sites are measured. Designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) for its populations of water birds, the reserve is particularly popular among birdwatchers. Its also well-known for its nightingales which "can be heard signing between the end of April and June." The range of birds, insects, mammals and flora is "one of the many reasons why Paxton Pits is such a special place", its website says. Each year between the end of April and June, visitors can hear the distinctive song of nightingales. The reserve also includes its very own visitor centre which houses a "great café" serving refreshments and other products. Unsurprisingly, it has received a tidal wave of rave reviews over the years, with visitors praising its "beautiful surroundings". One said: "We had a lovely walk around the site and then stopped for a hot chocolate and a muffin. The staff were lovely and everything was clean and tidy." Another added: "A lovely gem of a place, beautiful walks, amazing scenery, great café, clean, well organised and a great place to spend the day. We went on two different walks and really enjoyed them both." Paxton Pits Nature Reserve is just off the A1, making it a convenient stop for travellers and locals alike. What's your favourite walk in Cambridgeshire? Let us know in the comments. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: 10 Cambridgeshire criminals who were jailed in November
metadata.contentSnippet: Criminals jailed in Cambridgeshire in November 2026 include a serial shoplifter, gang members who supplied cocaine and a controlling partner.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 Cambridgeshire criminals who were jailed in November
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Here are some of the criminals who ended up behind bars across Cambridgeshire in November, including a serial shoplifter, gang members who supplied Cambridgeshire with cocaine and a controlling partner who subjected his victim to a decade of abuse. A serial shoplifter was jailed after targeting the same Fenland shop three days in a row. On August 30, Kallum Payne, 24, of Gaul Road, March, began a spree of thefts at the Superdrug store on Broad Street in March. He stole skincare products with a total value of £457.84 on three consecutive days without attempting to pay. On Tuesday, November 3, at Cambridge Crown Court, Payne was jailed for 18 months, having admitted five counts of theft from a shop. Kallum Payne stole skincare products valued at more than £400 (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A second robber was jailed for more than four years for attacking a group of boys in Peterborough and stealing a bicycle. Imran Ali, 41, was jailed for 50 months at Cambridge Crown Court on November 2. The sentence comes after he was found guilty of robbery and two counts of attempted robbery. Together with Declan Hyland, 29, and another man they ambushed the youngsters at around 5pm on April 18. Imran Ali was found guilty of robbery (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A convicted Cambridgeshire sex offender was jailed for breaching a court order after creating a secret social media account. Harry Yeardsley, 20, admitted two breaches of a Sexual Harm Prevention Order (SHPO). The order was imposed earlier this year after Yeardsley pleaded guilty to sexual communication with a child. Officers discovered that Yeardsley had created, used, and deleted an account on Kik. He was jailed for six months at Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on November 6. Yousif Nechirvan, 31, and Aras Abrahim, 35, were arrested on February 17 following four simultaneous police warrants at properties in Peterborough. They found 30 wraps of cocaine worth up to £900 concealed in a cigarette packet and £6,000 in cash hidden behind kitchen kickboards. Nechirvan, of Western Avenue, was jailed for three years and seven months and Abrahim, of Whalley Street, was jailed for 28 months. Yousif Nechirvan (left) and Aras Abrahim (right) (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A burglar who "repeatedly targeted" Cambridgeshire properties and stole more than £2,000 worth of alcohol was jailed. Darren Valentine, 35, of no fixed address, admitted three burglaries, five attempted burglaries, breaching a Criminal Behaviour Order and attempting to steal a car. On May 26, Valentine climbed into the rear garden of Margaret’s Cambridge on Chesterton Road and stole £400 worth of alcohol from its cellar. On August 29, he broke into a garage on Mariners Way in Chesterton and stole two bikes, an electric moped and £1,830 worth of alcohol. Valentine was jailed for 20 months at Peterborough Crown Court on November 5. Darren Valentine stole £2,000 worth of alcohol (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A controlling partner who subjected his victim to a decade of abuse and even strangled her was jailed for more than two years. Anthony Bernard, 49, of Croyland Road, Walton, Peterborough, pleaded guilty to engaging in controlling or coercive behaviour in an intimate or family relationship and intentional strangulation. His abuse came to light after an incident on August 11, when he emptied his partner’s wardrobe, took her belongings, and threatened to burn them in a car. Police uncovered more than a decade of coercive and controlling behaviour during their investigation. Bernard was jailed for two years and three months and given a restraining order at Cambridge Crown Court on Wednesday, November 4. Anthony Bernard strangled his victim in a decade of abuse (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A shoplifter was jailed after breaching a court order and going on a three-day stealing spree. Joshua Preece, 21, was sentenced to eight months at Huntingdon Magistrates’ Court on November 12 after admitting four counts of theft from a shop and two breaches of a criminal behaviour order (CBO). The thefts took place in Peterborough between October 30 and November 1, targeting M&S and Next at Brotherhood Retail Park and a BP filling station in Bretton. He also breached his two-year CBO by entering the Bretton Centre on October 26 and 31. Joshua Preece breached a court order (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) A shoplifter was jailed after threatening to stab staff with a drill bit at a Peterborough toy shop. Stephen Foot, 29, was confronted by staff at Smyths Toys in Boongate on November 3 when he was caught stealing a toy truck. He pulled out a pointed drill bit and threatened to stab staff if they approached him before fleeing the scene with the stolen item. At Peterborough Magistrates' Court on November 4, he was charged with possession of a bladed article and three counts of theft from a shop and sentenced to six months in prison. A man who stole an orangutan statue priced at more than £700 from a garden centre in Cambridgeshire was jailed for nearly two years. Derek Lundgren, 61, of New Road, Sawston, took the £799 statue from Scotsdales Garden Centre in Horningsea on September 7. He was captured on CCTV leaving the store without paying before jumping on his bike, placing the giant animal figure across the handlebars and cycling off. Lundgren was sentenced to a year and 11 months in prison (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) At Ipswich Magistrates’ Court on November 9, Lundgren was sentenced to a year and 11 months in prison.

metadata.title: Prominence regime risks your right to choose your news
metadata.contentSnippet: Would you prefer to choose the news and information you consume, or would you rather the Government decides for you?

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Prominence regime risks your right to choose your news
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Would you prefer to choose the news and information you consume, or would you rather the Government decides for you? The former allows you to exercise personal choice, judgement and agency. The latter would see the Government trying to take that freedom away and instead serve you news and information it has deemed suitable, relevant and appropriate. It’s confusing and deeply worrying, then, that the latter is what the Government’s proposed prominence regime is looking to do by giving the state a say over which sources of news are pushed up your social media feed, rather than leaving that choice to you. To me, that’s not the sort of edict we would expect in a world-leading democracy like ours, and certainly not in one led by a Prime Minister that has himself recently espoused the value of a free press. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy (Image: Maja Smiejkowska) Journalists are here to represent your interests and hold power to account on your behalf. Often, that means challenging authority in ways that may be uncomfortable or, at times, disruptive to what Government – local, regional or national – is seeking to achieve. So, we must resist any attempt by Government to control our free press. Any influence of Government over what journalists can publish is an erosion of this fundamental principle. This can happen in all sorts of ways. Not all erosion of free speech is an obvious, brutal clampdown. But when we see it in any form, we must act. Earlier this year, Ministers brought forward proposals to make what it describes as trusted sources of news more prominent on social media, in a bid to crack down on mis and disinformation which blights our online ecosystem. On the face of it, a worthy objective. But dig a little deeper and the proposals carry serious and fundamental risks. Firstly, selection of titles for prominence. Who would decide which titles are more prominent online and on what criteria? This matters enormously because deciding which titles receive greater prominence means deciding which sources get an advantage in reaching you, the reader. And whoever is making those decisions suddenly wields massive power and control of the information being read by millions of people every single day. This must not happen. No one should have that kind of power and most certainly not the Government - it’s for you the reader to decide what sources of news you consume, and that must not change. We don’t believe this Government intends to implement draconian censorship, but the power it is intending to give itself over the dissemination of news and topical information could easily be weaponised by future administrations with more nefarious and dangerous objectives. That is a dystopian nightmare. It could also narrow the range of news you see. Ranking is a zero-sum game: every title pushed up your feed pushes another down. A plural press depends on readers drawing on many different sources, but prominence would push in the opposite direction. The other big question here is how, from a technical and practical perspective, a prominence regime could possibly work for local news publishers serving hundreds of communities across the UK. I’m not sure, and I’m pretty sure the Government doesn’t know either. The obvious answer for such a regime is that it would have to involve highly invasive tracking of users with hundreds if not thousands of individual regulatory regimes running in parallel across the country. Otherwise, how could local news get to local people in areas where titles overlap? The regime would also disproportionately benefit the BBC, the UK’s publicly funded broadcaster. Let’s remember, the BBC is already hell bent on using its own licence-fee funded digital local news services to squash commercial local news providers. And, in reality, the tech platforms this regime relies on would just give prominence to the BBC because, on a technical level, it’s easier and why would they give themselves an undue headache? Some will say prominence is a way to take on the tech giants. But it would leave their grip on news firmly in place. The platforms would still own the algorithms, still decide how to comply, still surface mis- and disinformation - and still keep most of the value of the journalism that passes through their feeds. All the regime would add is the hand of the state on top. We are being offered a choice between platform power and state power. It is a false choice. Power should instead move to the people this is supposed to be about: you, the reader, and the publishers who produce the journalism you rely on. There is a better way. That means giving you the right to choose which news sources you see more of, and requiring the platforms to respect that choice. It means giving publishers transparency over how platforms rank their journalism and who it reaches, control over how it is presented, so they can build direct relationships with their audiences. And it means backing the Competition and Markets Authority in using its new digital markets powers to make sure the platforms pay fairly for the news they profit from, so publishers can sustain the journalism that keeps communities informed. Alongside that, the Government can make good on its promises to help local journalism thrive by diverting a greater share of central Government advertising to local news titles and keeping public notices in local news media. But prominence is not the right way forward. We have voiced our concerns but need your help to make our case. Contact your local MP today and be clear that you want to continue to choose your news. Theo Bamber, News Media Association Chief Executive

metadata.title: Gang members part of 'significant operation' to supply cocaine pictured
metadata.contentSnippet: Two members of a gang supplying cocaine in Peterborough have been jailed after four simultaneous raids.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Gang members part of 'significant operation' to supply cocaine pictured
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two members of a gang supplying cocaine in Cambridgeshire have been jailed. Yousif Nechirvan, 31, and Aras Abrahim, 35, were arrested on February 17 following four simultaneous police warrants at properties in Peterborough. Nechirvan was at home in Western Avenue, Dogsthorpe, when police arrived. They found 30 wraps of cocaine worth up to £900 concealed in a cigarette packet and £6,000 in cash hidden behind kitchen kickboards. An investigation revealed Nechirvan played a significant role in the conspiracy. He provided vehicles, maintained communications and possessed large quantities of class A drugs. When police conducted another warrant in Whalley Street, Eastfield, they found seven mobile phones linked to the drug line in Abrahim’s bedroom. Analysis of the mobile phones revealed bulk messages linked to the supply of cocaine. A third warrant was conducted in Fengate where Sartip Mustafa, 22, was arrested. Nearly 400 wraps of cocaine and a 67g block of the class A drug were discovered, worth up to a combined £16,500. They also discovered packaging materials, scales and other drug-related paraphernalia. Camila Teixeira, 21, was arrested during the final warrant in Eastfield Road, where officers found 40 wraps of cocaine worth up to £1,200. Teixeira’s fingerprints were also found on some of the cash seized from the property in Western Avenue. Detectives found evidence Teixeira was involved in the conspiracy as a drug runner. All four defendants were sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court Thursday (November 19) after admitting conspiring to supply cocaine. Nechirvan, of Western Avenue, was jailed for three years and seven months. Abrahim, of Whalley Street, was jailed for 28 months. Mustafa, of no known address, and Teixeira, of Eastfield Road, were both sentenced to two years in prison, suspended for two years. They were also ordered to complete 150 hours of unpaid work. DC James Hamilton said: "This was a significant operation supplying cocaine throughout Peterborough and the surrounding area. "Damning evidence found at each of the warrants, combined with what was uncovered during a thorough investigation, left the defendants with little choice but to admit their involvement in the conspiracy. "Class A drugs trap people in addiction and cause misery for our communities with associated crime such as violence, burglary and anti-social behaviour. "We will continue to relentlessly pursue those who choose to supply these substances in Cambridgeshire and bring them to justice." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Vacant shop unit on St Neots high street could become youth centre
metadata.contentSnippet: The former M&Co shop unit on St Neots high street could become a youth centre under a new planning application submitted by St Neots Town Council.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Vacant shop unit on St Neots high street could become youth centre
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A shop unit on St Neots high street could become a youth centre under a new planning application. St Neots Town Council wants to turn the vacant ground-floor unit at 25-27 Market Square, formerly an M&Co store, into a permanent youth services base. The former clothing shop was split in two, with Cook, the frozen food business, taking over the rear unit. But the front unit has been empty since April 2023 after failing to attract a buyer or tenant. The building would be transformed using Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) funding, pending approval. The centre would offer a youth café, drop-in club sessions, educational workshops, arts and recreation activities, health and wellbeing programmes, counselling and mentoring. It would also include offices for youth workers and partner organisations. A potential timetable of events for the space included in the planning documents reveals there would be a main room, activity room and meeting room. The proposal involves mainly internal alterations, with no significant changes to the building's appearance. A visual included with the application shows how the frontage could look if the youth centre is approved. A visual by Cameron Bosque Brookes Architects showing what the new frontage could look like (Image: HDC/Cameron Bosque Brookes Architects) According to planning documents, the facility would primarily cater to young people aged between eight and 17, although some activities could involve older participants. The council says demand for a dedicated youth facility is growing as St Neots expands through developments including Loves Farm, Wintringham and eastern expansion areas, but youth facilities have not kept pace. Supporting documents reveal that a district-wide youth survey, which included 673 young people, highlighted a demand for more youth clubs, safe indoor spaces, and places where young people could access support and form friendships. The centre would open six days a week: from 9am to 9pm Monday to Friday and from 9am to 7pm on Saturdays. Most youth activities would run between 3pm and 9pm on weekdays. Daytime sessions would focus on targeted services, counselling and work with partner organisations. Council documents estimate typical youth sessions would attract 15 to 50 young people, with a maximum occupancy of 71, including staff. Qualified youth workers and volunteers would staff the centre, with safeguards including controlled access, attendance records, CCTV and DBS checks where necessary. Full details on the application can be viewed using Huntingdonshire District Council's planning portal using reference 26/02136/FUL.

news.content: A new café and bistro could be on the cards for Ramsey if plans are approved. Turquazze Restaurant Ltd has submitted a fresh premises licence application to Huntingdonshire District Council. Bloom and Brew would operate from the unit previously occupied by Konak Café and Grill, on 34 Great Whyte. According to the applicant, the bistro would serve breakfast, lunch and dinner, including British and Mediterranean cuisine. "The premises has approximately 70 customer seats. Alcohol will be served indoors only, with meals, by waiter service at tables. "No off-sales of alcohol are proposed," the plans said. "Bloom and Brew will operate as a family-friendly café and restaurant. "Alcohol will only be served with meals, by waiter service at tables, staff will be trained in responsible alcohol sales, public safety and child protection. "The premises will be properly managed and supervised." If approved, the venue would serve alcohol for consumption on the premises between the hours of 8am and 10.30pm Monday to Sunday. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new café and bistro could be on the cards for Ramsey if plans are approved. Turquazze Restaurant Ltd has submitted a fresh premises licence application to Huntingdonshire District Council. Bloom and Brew would operate from the unit previously occupied by Konak Café and Grill, on 34 Great Whyte. According to the applicant, the bistro would serve breakfast, lunch and dinner, including British and Mediterranean cuisine. "The premises has approximately 70 customer seats. Alcohol will be served indoors only, with meals, by waiter service at tables. "No off-sales of alcohol are proposed," the plans said. "Bloom and Brew will operate as a family-friendly café and restaurant. "The premises will be properly managed and supervised." If approved, the venue would serve alcohol for consumption on the premises between the hours of 8am and 10.30pm Monday to Sunday. Members of the public can make representations concerning the application, either in writing or by email to licensing@huntingdonshire.gov.uk. metadata.title: Prisoner admits murdering Soham killer Ian Huntley after changing plea
metadata.contentSnippet: A whole-life prisoner at HMP Frankland Anthony Russell has admitted murdering "Soham killer" Ian Huntley after changing his plea.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Prisoner admits murdering Soham killer Ian Huntley after changing plea
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A whole-life prisoner has admitted murdering Soham killer Ian Huntley at a high-security jail after changing his plea. Anthony Russell went on trial at Newcastle Crown Court on November 23, accused of killing 52-year-old Huntley by swinging a 4kg metal bar at least six times at his head. The prosecution said it was a “cold-blooded murder” that he planned for weeks. On Tuesday, November 24, Russell, 44, asked to change his plea and admitted the single charge of murder. Already convicted of three murders, Russell launched the attack when the two men were working in the recycling workshop at HMP Frankland, near Durham, on February 26. Huntley died in hospital nine days later, having sustained a fractured skull and brain bleed and never having regained consciousness. Huntley murdered schoolgirls Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman in the Cambridgeshire town of Soham in August 2002. He was jailed for life and ordered to serve a minimum of 40 years after the girls' bodies were found two weeks after they had gone missing.

Issue 2 – Settlement Break 
 
4.14 In respect of Policy 2, Protected Settlement Break, both Huntingdonshire 
District Council and Savills, acting on behalf of David Wilson Homes South 
Midlands, have drawn attention to a live planning application, primarily for 
residential development, across the whole of this site.
20
  The proposed 
development includes an undeveloped landscape buffer with a minimum 
width of about 12m across the site’s southern boundary. In addition, an 
adjacent landscape buffer could be sought as part of the development of 
the RAF Upwood site to the south. 
 
4.15 Savills consider the policy fails the Basic Conditions.  Savills assert, inter 
alia, that in the absence of national and local planning policy specifically 
related to Protected Settlement Breaks (or similar), Local Green Space 
policy should be applied, principally the criteria set out in NPPF, Paragraph 
106.  Whilst I accept that the practical effect of both mechanisms is to 
restrict development, Local Green Space and Settlement Breaks fulfil 
distinctly separate planning purposes. Settlement breaks aim to maintain 
the physical and visual separation of distinct communities and prevent 
coalescence, whilst Local Green Space designations protect areas special 
to a local community—such as for beauty, historic significance, 
tranquillity, or wildlife.  
 
4.16 To my mind, to separate the settlements of Ramsey and Bury through a 
settlement break is a laudable objective.  Overall, I am satisfied ‘The 
Ramsey Settlement Boundary Methodology, April 2026’ provides a

Main Findings - Executive Summary

From my examination of the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (the Plan) and its supporting documentation, including the representations made, I have concluded that subject to the policy modifications set out in this report, the Plan meets the Basic Conditions.

I have also concluded that: - the Plan has been prepared and submitted for examination by a qualifying body – Ramsey Town Council; - the Plan has been prepared for an area properly designated – the Ramsey Neighbourhood Plan Area (Map 2 on Page 17 of the Plan); - the Plan specifies the period to which it is to take effect – 2026 – 2046; and - the policies relate to the development and use of land for a designated neighbourhood area.
I recommend that the Plan, once modified, proceeds to referendum on the basis that it has met all the relevant legal requirements.
I have considered whether the referendum area should extend beyond the designated area to which the Plan relates and have concluded that it should not.
1. Introduction and Background
The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan 2026 - 2046

1.1 The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan 2026 – 2046 covers the civil parish of Ramsey, located within Huntingdonshire District in the county of Cambridgeshire.  Included within the parish are the settlements of Ramsey itself together with Ramsey Forty Foot, Ramsey Heights, Ramsey Mereside, Ramsey St Mary’s, the area of Ramsey Hollow and a small part of Pondersbridge.  The parish is sited generally to the north- northeast of Huntingdon and south-southeast of Peterborough.

1.2 Since designation as a neighbourhood area by Huntingdonshire District Council in February 2024, work on the Plan has progressed under the direction of a steering group.  This was formed after holding a neighbourhood plan meeting to which all households were invited.  A further meeting and a community consultation survey followed. Throughout the exercise, publicity has been achieved through postcards to all households, a Facebook page, newsletter and local engagement events.
1.3 The resultant Plan has a broad vision, four objectives and 10 policies.  The policies fall into one of three themes: community, heritage and environment, and infrastructure.
Intelligent Plans and Examinations (IPE) Ltd, Office 10, 5 Argyle Street, Bath BA2 4BA Registered in England and Wales. Company Reg. No. 10100118. VAT Reg. No. 237 7641 84 5
The Independent Examiner

1.4  As the Plan has now reached the examination stage, I have been appointed as the examiner of the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan by Huntingdonshire District Council, with the agreement of Ramsey Town Council.

1.5  I am a chartered town planner and former government Planning Inspector with over forty years’ experience.  I have worked in both the public and the private sectors.  I am an independent examiner and do not have an interest in any of the land that may be affected by the draft Plan.
The Scope of the Examination

1.6  As the independent examiner, I am required to produce this report and recommend either: (a) that the neighbourhood plan is submitted to a referendum without changes; or (b) that modifications are made and that the modified neighbourhood plan is submitted to a referendum; or (c) that the neighbourhood plan does not proceed to a referendum on the basis that it does not meet the necessary legal requirements.

1.7  The scope of the examination is set out in Paragraph 8(1) of Schedule 4B to the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 (as amended) (“the 1990 Act”). The examiner must consider: • Whether the plan meets the Basic Conditions.

• Whether the plan complies with provisions under Section 38A and Section 38B of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004 (as amended) (“the 2004 Act”). These are: -  it has been prepared and submitted for examination by a qualifying body, for an area that has been properly designated by the local planning authority; - it sets out policies in relation to the development and use of land and does not go beyond the scope of what may be included in a draft plan 1 ;
- it specifies the period during which it has effect;
- it is the only neighbourhood plan for the area and does not relate to land outside the designated neighbourhood area;
- it does not include provisions and policies for “excluded development”;
1 See Section 38B(A1) and Section 38B(2C)(a) of the 2004 Act.

- so far as the qualifying body considers appropriate, and having regard to the subject matter of the plan, it takes account of any local nature recovery strategy, under section 104 of the Environment Act 2021, that relates to all or part of the neighbourhood area. 3
• Whether the referendum boundary should be extended beyond the designated area, should the plan proceed to referendum.
• Such matters as prescribed in the Neighbourhood Planning (General) Regulations 2012 (as amended) (“the 2012 Regulations”).

1.8  I have considered only matters that fall within Paragraph 8(1) of Schedule 4B to the 1990 Act, with one exception.  That is the requirement that the Plan is compatible with the Human Rights Convention.
The Basic Conditions

1.9  The “Basic Conditions” are set out in Paragraph 8(2) of Schedule 4B to the 1990 Act.  In order to meet the Basic Conditions, the neighbourhood plan must: -  have regard to national policies and advice contained in guidance issued by the Secretary of State;
- contribute to the achievement of sustainable development;

- not result in the development plan for the area of the authority proposing that less housing is provided by means of development taking place in that area than if the neighbourhood development plan were not to be made 4 ;

2 This additional requirement was commenced on 25 March 2026 by virtue of The Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023 (Commencement No. 11 and Saving and Transitional Provisions) Regulations 2026, which brought into force section 98 of the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023. 3 See footnote above. 4 This Basic Condition applies from 25 March 2026 by virtue of The Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023 (Commencement No. 11 and Saving and Transitional Provisions) Regulations 2026, which brought into force Section 99 of the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023.  This replaces the former Basic Condition which required a neighbourhood plan to be in general conformity with the strategic policies of the development plan for the area.

- meet prescribed conditions and comply with prescribed matters.

1.10  Regulation 32 of the 2012 Regulations prescribes a further Basic Condition for a neighbourhood plan.  This requires that the making of the Neighbourhood Development Plan does not breach the requirements of Chapter 8 of Part 6 of the Conservation of Habitats and Species Regulations 2017. 6

Qualifying Body and Neighbourhood Plan Area

Development and Use of Land

4. Compliance with the Basic Conditions
Assimilated Obligations

4.1  The Neighbourhood Plan was screened for Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) by consultants acting for Ramsey Town Council, which found that it was unnecessary to undertake SEA.  Having read the Strategic Environmental Assessment Screening Report, I support this conclusion.

4.2  The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan was further screened for Habitats Regulations Assessment (HRA), which also was not triggered. Main Issues

4.3  Having regard for the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan, the consultation responses and other evidence, and the site visit, I consider that there are seven main issues relating to the Basic Conditions for this examination.  These concern: - Built-up Area Boundary - Settlement Break; - Community Engagement - Local Green Space - Views and Vistas - Infrastructure Provision - Transport Matters

4.4 Before I deal with the main issues, I have a few observations to make with regard to the representations.  First, the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan should be seen in the context of the wider planning system.  This includes Huntingdonshire’s Local Plan to 2036 as well as the NPPF and PPG.  It is not necessary to repeat in the Neighbourhood Plan matters that are quite adequately dealt with elsewhere. 13 Having said that, there may be scope to give emphasis to matters particularly relevant in the context of Ramsey.

4.5 Secondly, the Neighbourhood Plan does not have to deal with each and every topic raised through the consultation.  In this regard, the content of the Neighbourhood Plan and the scope of the policies (including housing allocations) is largely at the discretion of the qualifying body, albeit informed by the consultation process and the requirements set by the Basic Conditions.

4.6 Thirdly, my central task is to judge whether the Neighbourhood Plan satisfies the Basic Conditions.  Many of the representations do not demonstrate or indicate a failure to meet those conditions or other legal requirements.  Similarly, many of the suggested additions and improvements are not necessary when judged against the Basic Conditions.
4.7 The following section of my report sets out modifications that are necessary in order to meet the Basic Conditions.  Some of the proposed

modifications are factual corrections. 14 Others are necessary in order to have closer regard to national policies and advice.  In particular, plans should be succinct and contain policies that are clearly written and unambiguous. 15 In addition, the policies should be supported by appropriate evidence. 16
Issue 1 – Built-up Area Boundary

4.8 Policy 1 of the Neighbourhood Plan defines a settlement boundary for Ramsey and other settlements.  In order to protect the countryside from encroachment, growth is directed to the built-up area of the settlements as defined by the settlement boundaries.

4.9 Huntingdonshire District Council is concerned that proposed or built rural exception sites are excluded from the built-up area boundaries and that opportunities for sustainable development could be compromised, contrary to the Local Plan.

4.10 For my part, I note that none of the settlements have any proposed or built rural exception sites. 17 Such sites could be developed in the future without compromising sustainable development and incorporated within settlement boundaries, where logical, upon future revision of the Neighbourhood Plan.

4.11 The second paragraph of Policy 1 states that applications will be expected to demonstrate how they have taken into account the existing built form, layout and structure of the surrounding area.  To my mind, the meaning of “structure” is not entirely clear.  In its response to my questions, the Town Council has clarified the meaning. 18 To add clarity to the policy, such an explanation should be included within the supporting text.

4.12 Under the policy, developments are also expected to take account of “views and vistas”.  The Town Council has confirmed that, in part, these are the views and vistas the subject of Policy 6. 19 However, the reference is not intended to prevent consideration of views and vistas that may become apparent during the design process.  In response, I would say that I have had the opportunity to consider the appropriateness of the views and vistas defined under Policy 6.  However, the same cannot be said of views and vistas that may emerge in the future.  The policy should be limited to views and vistas identified in Policy 6.
4.13 On a final point, the ultimate paragraph of Policy 1 states that land outside or not well related to the settlement boundary should be

14 Modifications for the purpose of correcting errors is provided for in Paragraph 10(3)(e) of Schedule 4B to the 1990 Act. 15 NPPF, Paragraphs 15 and 16 d). 16 PPG Reference ID: 41-041-20140306. 17 See Town Council’s answers dated 14 July 2026 to my questions. 18 See Town Council’s answers dated 14 July 2026 to my questions. 19 See Town Council’s answers dated 14 July 2026 to my questions.
Intelligent Plans and Examinations (IPE) Ltd, Office 10, 5 Argyle Street, Bath BA2 4BA Registered in England and Wales. Company Reg. No. 10100118. VAT Reg. No. 237 7641 84 13

determined in accordance with the relevant Local Plan and Neighbourhood Plan policies.  Strictly speaking, it is the development of such land that should accord with the policies.  In addition, the provision will relate to all development outside the settlement boundary, whether or not it is well related to the boundary.  This and other necessary amendments are the subject of proposed modification PM1.
Issue 2 – Settlement Break

4.14 In respect of Policy 2, Protected Settlement Break, both Huntingdonshire District Council and Savills, acting on behalf of David Wilson Homes South Midlands, have drawn attention to a live planning application, primarily for residential development, across the whole of this site. 20 The proposed development includes an undeveloped landscape buffer with a minimum width of about 12m across the site’s southern boundary. In addition, an adjacent landscape buffer could be sought as part of the development of the RAF Upwood site to the south.

4.15 Savills consider the policy fails the Basic Conditions.  Savills assert, inter alia, that in the absence of national and local planning policy specifically related to Protected Settlement Breaks (or similar), Local Green Space policy should be applied, principally the criteria set out in NPPF, Paragraph 106.  Whilst I accept that the practical effect of both mechanisms is to restrict development, Local Green Space and Settlement Breaks fulfil distinctly separate planning purposes. Settlement breaks aim to maintain the physical and visual separation of distinct communities and prevent coalescence, whilst Local Green Space designations protect areas special to a local community—such as for beauty, historic significance, tranquillity, or wildlife.

4.16 To my mind, to separate the settlements of Ramsey and Bury through a settlement break is a laudable objective.  Overall, I am satisfied ‘The Ramsey Settlement Boundary Methodology, April 2026’ provides a sufficiently comprehensive assessment of the rational and approach taken to defining the Protected Settlement Break and is robust.

4.17 The District Council considers that sufficient landscaping can be secured through the planning application and through a draft policy in the emerging Local Plan with regard to the RAF Upwood site (“Bury 3”) to provide the desired visual separation. Although the landscape buffer envisaged by the District Council could go some way to achieve visual separation, it would do nothing to prevent coalescence and achieve separation from the western fringe of Bury in the vicinity of the Longland Crescent area.  The overall objective of Policy 2 would not be met.

4.18 I am not recommending any modification of Policy 2.  I appreciate that, in the event of the planning application being approved by Huntingdonshire District Council, then the District Council’s solution remains the best
20 Planning Application Ref: 25/01382/OUT.
Intelligent Plans and Examinations (IPE) Ltd, Office 10, 5 Argyle Street, Bath BA2 4BA Registered in England and Wales. Company Reg. No. 10100118. VAT Reg. No. 237 7641 84 14

fallback option and modification in line with the “required change” would be the sensible course of action.  However, given what I have seen and read, it is not a solution that I would seek to promote as the preferred course of action.
Issue 3 – Community Engagement

4.19 I have two points of concern in relation to Policy 4, Community Engagement.  First, the policy refers to contact by developers with the Town Council to discuss pre-application community engagement. Although the wording says that developers “should” contact the Town Council, this cannot be required through a development plan policy.  An alternative form of wording is required.

4.20 Secondly, the policy indicates that applications that detail how the outcome of pre-application community engagement have been taken into account will be supported.  I appreciate that this form of wording has been used elsewhere.  However, to my mind, it is not sufficient to support a proposal just because the outcome of community engagement is detailed. The details should demonstrate a positive response.  The two necessary amendments are addressed in proposed modification PM2.
Issue 4 – Local Green Space

4.21 Under Policy 5, five sites would be allocated as Local Green Spaces (LGS). With particular regard to Site E, Ramsey Forty Foot Moorings, Huntingdonshire District Council is concerned that LGS designation could create an unnecessary policy barrier to the delivery of flood mitigation infrastructure, open space and moorings access.

4.22 I note that proposals to improve mooring infrastructure and to improve public access are already supported through the policy.  Explicit support for flood mitigation infrastructure and suitable community infrastructure could be ensured through simple amendment, as proposed by the Town Council. 21

4.23 In all other respects, I am satisfied that the proposed designations meet the criteria and other considerations for designation, as set out in Paragraphs 106 to 108 of the NPPF.  They can be supported subject to proposed modifications PM3.
Issue 5 – Views and Vistas

4.24 Policy 6 of the Neighbourhood Plan concerns views and vistas.  Vista J is towards the golf course, across the settlement break in the Bury Neighbourhood Plan.  In this way, the policy attempts to control the potential loss of views across land that is outside the boundary of the Ramsey Neighbourhood Plan Area.  The Plan has no locus outside its
21 See Town Council’s answers dated 14 July 2026 to my questions.
Intelligent Plans and Examinations (IPE) Ltd, Office 10, 5 Argyle Street, Bath BA2 4BA Registered in England and Wales. Company Reg. No. 10100118. VAT Reg. No. 237 7641 84 15
designated area.  The related views cannot be controlled in this way. View/Vista J should be omitted from the Neighbourhood Plan.

4.25 In regard to View/Vista O, this runs along the boundary of the Neighbourhood Area. 22 It should be made clear that control is exercised only over proposals within the Ramsey Neighbourhood Plan Area. Proposed modification PM4 refers to these two matters.
Issue 6 – Infrastructure Provision

4.26 In Policy 7, Infrastructure Provision, it is clear that the words “where appropriate” are intended to cover the need for contributions to meet the tests for planning obligations. 23 However, the reference should apply to the circumstances of the application, not to the proposals as such. Focused amendment is necessary.
4.27 With regard to the provision of water and drainage infrastructure, this should be, if it is a necessity, expressed as a requirement.  Proposed modification PM5 applies to these two matters.
Issue 7 – Transport Matters

4.28 Policy 8 of the Neighbourhood Plan requires proposals to consider how development can contribute to the delivery of the provision of a network of walking and cycling linkages to the key services and facilities in the relevant town or village.  However, for clarity, details should be added of the existing network towards which development proposals can contribute.
4.29 The Town Council has provided details of an existing network. 24 This network should be referenced in a footnote to the policy and a copy provided within the Neighbourhood Plan.

4.30 Under the fourth paragraph of the policy, major developments will be supported where they secure improvements to public transport provisions. The words “where appropriate” should be added to make clear that the provision of improvements will be subject to the tests for planning obligations and the like.
4.31 The various necessary amendments are included in proposed modification PM6.

4.32 In the opening paragraph of Policy 9, Highway Impact, there is a reference to seeking contributions through planning obligations or planning conditions.  In this regard, planning obligations are the principal
22 See Section 38A(2) of the 2004 Act. 23 See Town Council’s answers dated 14 July 2026 to my questions. 24 See Town Council’s answers dated 14 July 2026 to my questions.
Intelligent Plans and Examinations (IPE) Ltd, Office 10, 5 Argyle Street, Bath BA2 4BA Registered in England and Wales. Company Reg. No. 10100118. VAT Reg. No. 237 7641 84 16
way in which financial contributions can be sought.  The text should be amended as in proposed modification PM7.
Other Policies

4.33 There are two policies that have not been the subject of commentary in the above report.  These are Policy 3, Community Facilities and Policy 10, Rights of Way Network.  To a greater or lesser extent, these topics are covered in NPPF Section 8 (Promoting healthy and safe communities).
4.34 Subject to the modifications that I have recommended, I find that there has been regard for national policy and that the Basic Conditions have been met.
Minor Amendments and Updates

4.35 Minor amendments to the text and numbering (sections, paragraphs etc) can be made consequential to the recommended modifications, alongside any other minor non-material changes or updates, in agreement between Huntingdonshire District Council and Ramsey Town Council. 25
5. Conclusions
Summary

5.1  The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan has been duly prepared in compliance with the procedural requirements.  My examination has investigated whether the Plan meets the Basic Conditions and other legal requirements for neighbourhood plans.  I have had regard for all the responses made following consultation on the Neighbourhood Plan, and the evidence documents submitted with it.

5.2  I have made recommendations to modify a number of policies and text to ensure the Plan meets the Basic Conditions and other legal requirements. I recommend that the Plan, once modified, proceeds to referendum.
The Referendum and its Area

5.3  I have considered whether or not the referendum area should be extended beyond the designated area to which the Plan relates.  The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan, as modified, has no policy or proposals which I consider significant enough to have an impact beyond the designated Neighbourhood Plan boundary, requiring the referendum to extend to areas beyond the Plan boundary.  I recommend that the boundary for the purposes of any future referendum on the Plan should be the boundary of the designated Neighbourhood Plan Area.
25 PPG Reference ID: 41-106-20190509.
Intelligent Plans and Examinations (IPE) Ltd, Office 10, 5 Argyle Street, Bath BA2 4BA Registered in England and Wales. Company Reg. No. 10100118. VAT Reg. No. 237 7641 84 17
Overview

5.4  It is evident that a considerable amount of time and effort has been devoted to the development and production of this Plan and I congratulate those who have been involved.  The Plan should prove to be a useful tool for future planning and change in Ramsey over the coming years.
Andrew S Freeman
Examiner
Intelligent Plans and Examinations (IPE) Ltd, Office 10, 5 Argyle Street, Bath BA2 4BA Registered in England and Wales. Company Reg. No. 10100118. VAT Reg. No. 237 7641 84 18

Ramsey Forty Foot Moorings), replace the second sentence with: “Proposals to improve mooring infrastructure, install flood mitigation infrastructure and to improve public access including suitable community infrastructure will be supported.” PM4 Page 75 From Policy 6, delete View/Vista J.  Carry out consequential amendments elsewhere in the Plan. At the beginning of the policy, add the words: “In regard to land within the Ramsey Neighbourhood Plan Area, proposals...”.

Replace the third paragraph of the policy with the following: “Development proposals will be supported where they can demonstrate that there is capacity in the local surface water drainage system, the water supply network and the sewerage network, or capacity can be made available in time to support the development, having regard to the advice of Anglian Water.” PM6 Page 88 In the third paragraph of Policy 8, following reference to a network of walking and cycling linkages, add a footnote referencing the Ramsey Market Town Transport Strategy. RAMSEY TOWN COUNCIL 
 
You are hereby summoned to attend a meeting of Ramsey Town Council to be held at 7pm 
on Thursday 10th September 2026, in The Lavender Room, Ramsey Town Council, 
Great Whyte, Ramsey, when the following items of business will be transacted: - 
 
Please ensure all mobile phones are switched off or turned to silent during the 
meeting. 
The meeting room will open to the public at 18.50. 
 
Lisa Renfree                                      4th September 2026 
   
  
 
  
Town Clerk/RFO 
 
A G E N D A  
 
 
APOLOGIES FOR ABSENCE 
 
1. DECLARATIONS OF INTEREST 
To receive declarations from Members as to disclosable pecuniary and other 
interests and the nature of those interests in relation to any agenda item. 
   
2. PUBLIC PARTICIPATION 
    To allow 20 minutes for any members of the public to address the Council.  
 
3. MINUTES 
To approve as a correct record, the Minutes of the meeting of the Council held on 
27
th
 August 2026 - attached. 
 
4. DISTRICT & COUNTY COUNCILLOR UPDATE: 
Cllrs H Tobias, K Maheshwari and R Coogan have been invited to address Town 
Council Members. 
 
5. PLANNING 
1.1 26/01440/FUL Change of use to a SEN day school (Class F1), erection of a 
rear single storey extension, external alterations to existing two-storey rear 
extension and associated works including additional car parking, new 
landscaping and recreation areas – Westward House, Bury Road, Ramsey. 
1.2 26/01089/HHFUL Proposed replacement roof to form first floor 
accommodation, demolition of the existing porch and erection of a new single 
storey porch, erection of a new balcony, installation of external insulation and 
cladding to the existing dwelling and associated internal alterations – Living 
Accommodation Stokes Garage, Ramsey Road, Ramsey Forty Foot. 
 
 
 Planning – other business 
a) Local Plan 2047 - Update  
b) Neighbourhood Plan Independent Inspector Report Update. 
 
 

6. FINANCE ITEMS 
a) Financial Summary - Cash book to 31/8/26 to be noted– to be tabled. 
b) Expenditure Transactions to be approved– to be tabled. 
c) To approve the implementation of the Local Government Pay Award - Pay rates 
and allowances have been increased by 3.3% with effect from 1
st
 April 2026.  
d) Updated Grant Form  
 
  
7. FUTURE SCOOTER PERMISSION 
Future Scooter would like to hold one to one training session on the QEII Skate 
Park and are seeking permission from Ramsey Town Council. 
 
 
8. WORKING PARTY UPDATES  
Members to receive an update from the Chair of each Working Party- circulated, to 
be noted. 
 
Communications Working Party 
Recommendation: 
Draft newsletter - to be tabled 
 
9. TOWN MAYOR’S AND CLERK’S CORRESPONDENCE: 
a) Just Giving Fire Fighter Fund Update 
b) FOI Response on CIL Funding Update. 
c) Emergency Planning Meeting – 1
st
 October 6:30pm at Ramsey Community 
Centre. 
d) Climate Emergency Briefing- 23
rd
 September at St Thomas a Becket Church 
6pm. 
e) Council to decide on centralised headstones in the lawn cemetery 
 
10. ATTENDANCES AT MEETINGS AND ORGANISATIONS: 
a) 1940 Drumhead Service 
b) Heritage Day – Councillor Support. 
 
11. DISTRICT WIDE DOG PSPO RENEWAL – CONSULTATION,  
Council to respond. 
 
12. MEETING DATES 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council (Planning) will take place on 24th 
September 2026 at 7pm.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

MINUTES OF RAMSEY TOWN COUNCIL MEETING 
held at 7pm on Thursday 27 August 2026 at  
Ramsey Town Council Great Whyte, Ramsey 
 
 
Present:  Councillors: I Axelsen, J Bufton, J Clarke, M Clarke, V Fendley (Mayor), S Fice, R Terrill, J 
Thompson, and  L Webster. 
In attendance: Mrs A Jerrom, Deputy Town Clerk  
 
The Chairman welcomed new Councillor Jessie Thompson to the meeting. 
 
289. Apologies for Absence. 
Cllrs J Aubin, A Austin, S Corney, A Costello, L Knight, C Maskell and P Rose. 
 
290.To Receive Declarations of Interest. 
No declarations of interest were made. 
 
291. Public Participation. 
There were no members of the public present. 
 
292. Minutes of the Last Meeting to be Approved. 
Councillors voted with two abstentions to accept the Minutes of the meeting of the Council held on 13
th
 
August 2026 as a correct record. 
 
293. Planning Applications for Consideration. 
1.1 26/01416/HHFUL – Two storey extension, barn and carport, internal and external alterations, new 
dormer and canopy roofs and installation of solar PV panels – Heathfield, Benwick Road, Ramsey Forty 
Foot    Proposed  by  Cllr  S  Fice  and  seconded  by  Cllr  L  Webster  Ramsey  Town  Council  voted 
unanimously for Huntingdonshire District Council to APPROVE the application as per their decision on 
a previous application for the property in June 2026, which had since been withdrawn. 
1.2  26/01206/OUT – Proposed demolition of an existing dwelling and outbuilding and replacement with 
4 new dwellings (outline application with all matters reserved, with the exception of access) – 190 Herne 
Road, Ramsey St Marys.  Having been proposed by Cllr J Clarke and seconded by Cllr Terrill, councillors 
voted  unanimously  to  recommend  refusal  of  the  application  due  to  the  lack  of  information  regarding 
adequate parking, particularly for the bungalows at the rear of the development.  They also had concerns 
regarding the possible precedent that might be set for development at the rear of properties in the village. 
1.3 26/01484/TREE – G1  (dead  Silver  Birch) – fell  and  remove – Cedar  Lodge,  St  Marys  Road, 
Ramsey.  Having  been  proposed  by  Cllr  S  Fice  and  seconded  by  Cllr  L  Webster  councillors  voted 
unanimously to make no observations either in favour or against the proposal but to leave the decision 
to the arboricultural officer. 
 
294.  Consultation on the Reviewed Bury Draft Neighbourhood Plan. 
Councillors discussed the suggested response to the consultation previously circulated by Cllr Fendley. 
It was agreed that there would be infrastructure implications for Ramsey following the growth within the 
Bury Neighbourhood Plan area. It was therefore proposed by Cllr Bufton, seconded by Cllr Terrill and 
agreed with one abstention to submit that response from the Town Council which included the 
acknowledgment of the need for Infrastructure Levy(CIL) contributions towards car parking provision at 
Mews Close and electric charging points which would serve the wider community. 
 
 
 
295. Update on Emergency Response – Holme Fen. 
Councillor Fendley provided an update on the huge operation to support the Fire Service while they 
were attending the recent fires at Holme Fen.  In answer to a request for emergency assistance from 
HDC the Mayor and Town Clerk had organised for food supplies to be provided to the firemen 
alongside that already organised by the Admiral Wells in Holme and Cllr Fendley had set up a Go 
Fund Me page for donations. There had been an amazing response from the community, with 
volunteers and local businesses providing food over the weekend and following days.  Cllr Fendley 
reported that the firemen had been overwhelmed by the response and hard work of all concerned and 
they would be issuing formal letters of thanks. There would be a further update on the Go Fund Me 

funds at the next meeting of the Town Council.  The Chief Fire Officer had been invited to attend the 
Mayor’s Civic Service in September. 
 
296. Meeting Dates 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council would take place on Thursday 10th September at 7pm.

RAMSEY TOWN COUNCIL 
 
You are hereby summoned to attend a meeting of Ramsey Town Council to be held at 7pm 
on Thursday 22nd October 2026, in The Lavender Room, Ramsey Town Council, Great 
Whyte, Ramsey, when the following items of business will be transacted: - 
 
Please ensure all mobile phones are switched off or turned to silent during the 
meeting. 
The meeting room will open to the public at 18.50. 
 
Lisa Renfree                                      16th October 2026 
   
  
 
  
Town Clerk/RFO 
 
A G E N D A  
 
 
APOLOGIES FOR ABSENCE 
 
1. DECLARATIONS OF INTEREST 
To receive declarations from Members as to disclosable pecuniary and other 
interests and the nature of those interests in relation to any agenda item. 
   
2. PUBLIC PARTICIPATION 
    To allow 20 minutes for any members of the public to address the Council.  
 
3. MINUTES 
To approve as a correct record, the Minutes of the meeting of the Council held on 
8
th
 October 2026 - attached. 
  
4. COUNCILLOR RESIGNATIONS 
Notice is hereby given pursuant to section 87(2) of the Local Government Act 1972 
that due to the resignation of Councillor Ash Austin and Councillor Phil Rose there 
are two vacancies in the Town Council. 
If, within 14 statutory days after the date of this notice, a request for an election to 
fill the vacancy is made in writing to the Returning Officer, Huntingdonshire District 
Council,  Pathfinder  House,  Huntingdon  PE29  3TN  by  ten  electors  of  the town  an 
election will be held.  If no such notice is given the Town Council will fill the vacancy 
by co-option. 
 
5. PLANNING- Members are asked to visit the Huntingdonshire District Council 
Planning Portal to view the plans and documents prior to the meeting. 
 
1.1 26/01809/FUL Erection of a new 2 bed bungalow, 284 Herne Road, Ramsey St 
Mary’s Huntingdon PE26 2TB 
1.2  26/01440/FUL Change of use to a SEN day school (Class F1), erection of a rear 
single storey extension, external alterations to existing two-storey rear extension, 
and associated works including additional car parking, new landscaping, and 
recreation areas, Westward House, Bury Road, Ramsey, Huntingdon PE26 1NA 
1.3 26/01526/FUL Temporary permission for a period of 15 years for the erection of 3 
units for use as retail or community space and associated public realm and 

highway improvements – Pedestrian Island, Great Whyte, Ramsey. This item is on 
the agenda to complete the vote on the substantial motion on 1.1 from the meeting 
of 8
th
 October. The substantive motion is ‘There is insufficient information for 
Ramsey Town Council to be able to support the application.’ If this vote is 
defeated it will return to the original motion ‘To accept the application’ 
 
 Planning – other business 
a) Feedback on Planning online training 21
st
 October. 
b) Feedback on the Development Management Committee reference the David 
Wilson Homes. Cllr S Corney 
c) To agree the representations to be submitted to Huntingdonshire District 
Council in response to their Local Plan consultation (previously circulated) 
 
 
6. MEETING DATES 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council will take place on 12th November 2026 at 
7pm.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
MINUTES OF RAMSEY TOWN COUNCIL MEETING 
held at 7pm on Thursday 08 October 2026 at  
Ramsey Town Council Great Whyte, Ramsey 
 
 
Present:    Councillors: A Austin, I Axelsen, J Bufton, J Clarke, M Clarke, Cllrs S Corney, V 
Fendley (Mayor), S Fice, L Knight, P Rose, R Terrill, J Thompson, L Webster and E Welsh. 
In attendance: Mrs L Renfree, Town Clerk  
 
320. Apologies for Absence. 
 Cllrs A Costello, C Maskell. 
 
321.To Receive Declarations of Interest. 
No declarations of interest were made at that point. 
 
322. Public Participation. 
There  was  six  members  of  the  public  who  discussed  planning  1.3,  discussing  the  potential 
199  David  Wilson  Homes  which  was  going  to  be  debated  on  19
th
 October  at  Development 
Management Panel and a question was raised to be answered post that meeting on where 
the community would stand to make a legal challenge. 
 
323. Minutes of the Last Meeting to be Approved. 
Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by Cllr L Knight, Councillors voted 13 FOR and 2 
ABSTENSIONS for the Minutes of the meeting of the Council held on 24
th
 September 2026 
as a correct record. 
 
324.County and District Councillor Update. 
County and District Councillor Cllr H Tobias attended the meeting to feedback on both County 
and District matters. Cllr Tobias outlined two visits to Ashbeach School and Abbey College 
and  commented  on  the  challenges  that  Ashbeach  faced  with  lack  of  SEN  funding  and 
commented on the brilliant discipline of the students in behaviour at Abbey College. As the 
County Councillor Cllr Tobias had been out with the Highways Officer to discuss the state of 
the roads in the community, and the biggest block is the funding to repair underneath the roads 
instead they are only able to fund patching them. Cllr Tobias then went on to discuss the 199 
David Wilson Homes and informed members that further housing would be coming at the RAF 
Upwood   site   and   still   with   no   infrastructure   in   place.   Cllr   Tobias   touched   on   the 
Pedestrianisation and welcomed better communication on the project. Cllr Tobias was asked 
by the Mayor if he had any information on the pilot project on resurfacing the Fen Roads – Cllr 
Tobias  had  not.  Cllr  J  Clarke  asked  Cllr  Tobais  about  the  waste  of  resource  on  the  use  of 
traffic  lights  when  no  work  is  taking  place.  Cllr  Tobias  noted  the  comments.  Cllr  Tobias did 
state you can read what he had been achieving in his two columns in the local newspaper. 
 
Presentation from Ramsey Neighbourhoods Trust 
Cllr I Axelsen and Cllr J Aubin declared a non-pecuniary interest on this item as Trustees of 
Ramsey Neighbourhoods Trust. 
 
Sam and Sarah from Ramsey Neighbourhoods Trust gave a presentation to members with an 
overview of the community group, what they do and what services they provide. Sarah talked 
through the young people’s projects which Ramsey Town Council funding had been covering. 
Cllr Axelsen who is also the Chair of Ramsey Neighbourhoods Trust had previously circulated 
the funding figures to members. The funding for the following year would be discussed at the 
following Finance Working Party and form part of the 20278/28 budget. 

 
 
325. Planning Applications for Consideration: 
 
1.1 26/01526/FUL Temporary permission for a period of 15 years for the erection of 3 units 
for use as retail or community space and associated public realm and highway 
improvements – Pedestrian Island, Great Whyte, Ramsey. Proposed by Cllr S Corney 
and seconded by Cllr E Welsh Cllr S Corney proposed acceptance of the application. 
Proposed by Cllr A  Austin and seconded by Cllr M Clarke an amendment to Cllr s 
Corney’s proposal ‘There is insufficient information for Ramsey Town Council to be able 
to support the application.’ A vote was taken on the amendment 5 FOR, 3 AGAINST and 
6 ABSTENSIONS. This meant that the amendment became the substantive motion. 
There was confusion for the councillors who voted to abstain as they thought they would 
then be able to vote on the original proposal by Cllr S Corney, this was not the case once 
the amendment had become the substantive motion. The meeting then moved on to 
planning application 1.2  
1.2 25/01301/FUL Erection of owner/site managers dwelling to serve existing caravan site.  
The retention of 14 existing touring caravan pitches, toilet and shower block and 3 holiday 
lodges along with the erection of two new timber holiday lodges and four new holiday 
pods – Riverside Lake and Leisure, Mereside Drove, Ramsey Mereside. Proposed by Cllr 
S Corney and seconded by Cllr P Rose Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for 
the District Council to APPROVE the application. Members were clear their previous 
comments still stood. 
1.3 26/01763/FUL Erection of 3 detached dwellings, 3 detached double garages and 
associated works – Oak Cottage, Forty Foot Bank, Ramsey Forty Foot. Cllrs A Austin, P 
Rose and S Corney declared a non-pecuniary interest as they knew the applicant. 
Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by Cllr J Bufton for District Council to 
APPROVE the application - Ramsey Town Council voted 6 FOR, 8 AGAINST and 1 
ABSTENTION The majority vote was for the application to be REFUSED. Members 
shared the concerns of the neighbouring residents in attendance. 
1.4 26/01763/FUL/26/01764/LBC Proposed conversion and extension of existing curtilage 
listed outbuilding into a separate, independently owned dwellinghouse – Bodsey House, 
Bodsey Toll Road, Ramsey. Proposed by Cllr L Knight and seconded by Cllr P Rose 
Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for the District Council to APPROVE the 
application 
1.5 25/01433/FUL /26/00045/REFUSL Land Far West of Romany Cottage, Bucks Drove, 
Ramsey St Marys. Proposed self-build dwelling to be used as site manager’s house.  
Appeal against refusal. Cllr J Clarke declared a non-pecuniary as a neighbour to the 
applicant. Proposed by Cllr M Clarke and seconded Ramsey Town Council 13 FOR and 2 
ABSTENTIONS for the District Council to keep the REFUSAL in place. Their previous 
comments stood. 
 
326. Planning – other business 
a) Latest Planning Tracker – noted 
b) Planning online training- Members were reminded of the online planning training that 
would take place on zoom on 21
st
 October 2026. The Clerk was asked to circulate the 
invitation again. 
 
327. Finance Items 
a) Financial summary – Cash book to 30/09/2026 – noted 

b) Expenditure Transactions to be approved. Proposed by Cllr S Corney and seconded by 
Cllr S Fice Ramsey Town Council voted UNANIMOUSLY for the expenditure transactions 
to be APPROVED. 
c) Grant applications – The Clerk informed members that 13 applications had been 
received and they would go to the next Finance Working Party and approved at the 
November Full Council meeting. 
d) Budget 2027/28 – Cllr S Fice informed members that the budget packs would be sent 
out in the following week. 
 
328.Working Party Updates 
 Members to receive an update from the Chairs of each Working Party – the Clerk 
apologised it had not gone out with the agenda papers but circulated that day. 
 
329. Working Party Recommendations 
 Economic Development – Members were informed that the SLA agreement for the 
Discover Huntingdonshire website. 
 Communications – Members were informed that the Newtown Road Play Park 
Consultation had been completed and the response was overwhelmingly positive. 
 
330.Town Mayor’s and Clerk’s Correspondence 
a) Civic Service Feedback – Cllr V Fendley fed back to members on how much people 
appreciated the Civic Service and its community spirit and that a lovely handwritten letter had 
been received by the High Sheriff of Cambridgeshire which would be in the office if any 
member wished to read it. 
b) Zebra Crossing Location, Abbey College Local Highways Initiative Bid – Members were 
informed by Cllr V Fendley that the wording on the consultation had been changed as 
Ramsey Town Council had not supported the zebra crossing due to the loss of parking 
spaces it would cause outside St Thomas a Becket Church. The Clerk was asked to forward 
the link to members. 
c) Local Highways Initiative Bid (Ramsey St Mary’s Buffer zones) update. The Clerk tabled 
the information received from Highways that the bid had not been successful. Further 
clarification had been asked for and it would go to the Amenities, Highways and Leisure 
Working Party. 
d) FOI Feedback – The Clerk informed members that the FOI had been responded to and no 
further communication had taken place. 
e) Newsletter Distribution – The Clerk informed members that the newsletter was being 
distributed and being well received. 
f) Development Management Committee – The Mayor informed members that the DMC 
meeting would take place on the 19
th
 October and members could attend in person, register 
to speak, or watch via zoom. Cllr S Corney would be representing the views at the meeting of 
Ramsey Town Council. 
g) Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan – The Mayor informed members that the 
referendum for the NHP would take place on Thursday 26
th
 November 2026. 
 
331. Car Park Land Lease 
To discuss the Heads of Terms for the lease – the Clerk had previously circulated the Heads 
of Terms for comment. Cllr J Clarke asked if the Clerk could push for a longer lease than 50 
years. No other comments were asked to be sent back to HDC. Once the lease has gone 
through HDC Legal it will come to members for sign off. 
 
332. Attendances at Meetings and Organisations 
a) Flood Action Planning Meeting – Cllr J Thompson fed back to members about the meeting 
and that the flood action group should be community led, focussed, and tested. 

b) Emergency Planning for the Future – Cllr V Fendley informed members that the meeting 
had 16 residents in attendance a very robust discussion had taken place. Cllr J Thompson 
had taken on the responsibility of outing the actions into the provided template. 
c) LVEP Conference – Cllr V Fendley explained the LVEP positioning starting at the bottom 
with Discover Ramsey, then Discover Huntingdonshire, Loval Visitor Economy Partnership 
and topped by Visit England. Cllr L Knight fed back to members about the Local Visitor 
Economy Forum Conference. It was a very positive meeting with a shout out to Ramsey for 
signing the Service Level Agreement for Discover Huntingdonshire. Both Cllr L K night and 
Cllr V Fendley both attended and sat on the table with Visit England. 
 
333. Meeting Dates 
The next meeting of Ramsey Town Council would take place on Thursday 22nd October 
(Planning) at 7pm. 
 
 
Town Mayor_______________________________________Date___________________

metadata.title: Nationwide confirms major change for millions of current account customers
metadata.contentSnippet: Nationwide Building Society is rolling out in-app transaction notifications to all customers, with SMS alerts continuing for those without the app.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Nationwide confirms major change for millions of current account customers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nationwide Building Society is rolling out in-app transaction notifications. The new feature will be introduced for all current account holders in the coming weeks, with customers receiving a notification via the app once it becomes available. Nationwide said: "In-app transaction notifications will be rolled out to all current account customers over the coming weeks. "You'll be notified via the app when this functionality is available to you." The change was first spotted by a member who noticed new options in the Nationwide mobile app and asked about the feature on social media. Nationwide already uses push notifications for other account updates. Guidance on Nationwide’s website states: "If you have the Nationwide app on your device and notifications enabled, you'll get alerts as notifications. "These are short messages sent by an app to your phone, even when the app isn't open." Customers are encouraged to ensure push notifications are enabled in their phone settings to avoid missing important updates. Those without the app will continue to receive alerts via SMS, provided Nationwide has a mobile number on file. The building society does not charge for these text messages. Nationwide said it was increasing rates across most of its variable-rate savings accounts from December 1. Among the changes, its 1 Year Triple Access Saver and 1 Year Triple Access ISA will both pay 3.55%, up from 3.30%. Members with a Reward Single Access ISA will see their rate increase from 2.80% to 3.05%, while Reward Saver and Reward ISA rates will rise from 2.75% to 3%. Other changes include: Rates on some instant-access accounts will also increase by up to 0.15 percentage points. Nationwide members signed up to its SavingsWatch service will be notified of changes affecting their accounts on December 1.
